title: Neutral Grip Fundamentals
body: A neutral grip positions the hands so the V's formed by thumb and forefinger point toward your trail shoulder. This promotes a square clubface at impact without manipulation. Check: you should see 2-2.5 knuckles on your lead hand at address. Benefits: consistent ball flight, reduced timing dependency. Common mistake: gripping too tight—maintain pressure of 4-5 on a 10 scale.

title: Strong Grip: When and Why
body: A strong grip rotates both hands clockwise (for right-handers) on the club, promoting a closed face through impact. Use when: fighting a slice, seeking a draw, or playing in wind requiring lower flight. Checkpoint: 3+ knuckles visible on lead hand. Caution: too strong can cause hooks and pulls. Pair with slightly open stance to balance.

title: Weak Grip for Fade Players
body: A weak grip rotates hands counterclockwise, opening the face through impact. Use when: seeking a fade, fighting hooks, or needing high soft shots. Checkpoint: only 1-1.5 knuckles visible on lead hand. This grip requires more hand rotation to square the face—better for players with fast hand action. Pair with slightly closed stance for balance.

title: Grip Pressure Control
body: Grip pressure affects clubhead speed and release timing. Light pressure (3-4/10) promotes speed and natural release. Tight pressure (7-8/10) restricts wrist hinge and slows the club. Ideal: firm enough to control the club, light enough to feel the clubhead. Test: if your forearms are tense at address, lighten up. Maintain consistent pressure throughout the swing.

title: Athletic Posture at Address
body: Good posture creates balance and allows rotation. Bend from the hips (not waist), keeping spine straight with slight knee flex. Arms hang naturally—hands should be about a fist-width from thighs. Weight balanced 50/50 or slightly toward balls of feet. Checkpoints: shoulders over toes, slight chin lift to allow shoulder turn. Feel athletic, like a shortstop ready to move.

title: Spine Angle and Tilt
body: Spine angle at address should match your club length—more upright for wedges, more bent for driver. Side tilt: trail shoulder slightly lower than lead due to trail hand position on grip. Maintain spine angle through impact—early extension (standing up) causes thin shots and blocks. Drill: practice swings with head against wall to feel maintained posture.

title: Alignment Fundamentals
body: Alignment means aiming your body and clubface at the target. Clubface aims at target; feet, hips, and shoulders align parallel left (for right-handers)—like railroad tracks. Common mistake: aligning feet at target pushes aim right. Use alignment sticks in practice. On course: pick intermediate target 2-3 feet ahead on your line.

title: Closed Stance for Draws
body: A closed stance (feet aimed right of target for right-handers) promotes an in-to-out swing path, encouraging draws. Use when: wanting right-to-left ball flight, fighting slice, hitting into right-to-left wind. Setup: close stance 5-10 degrees, keep clubface at target. Ball flight: starts right, curves left. Caution: too closed can cause pushes and hooks.

title: Open Stance for Fades
body: An open stance (feet aimed left of target) promotes out-to-in path, encouraging fades. Use when: wanting left-to-right ball flight, fighting hooks, or hitting into left-to-right wind. Setup: open stance 5-10 degrees, clubface at target. Ball flight: starts left, curves right. Also useful for short game shots requiring high, soft landing.

title: Stance Width by Club
body: Stance width affects stability and rotation. Driver: inside of feet at shoulder width or slightly wider. Irons: narrower, inside of feet at hip width. Wedges: narrowest, promoting control over power. Too wide restricts hip turn; too narrow reduces stability. Adjust for conditions: wider in wind for balance, narrower for punch shots.

title: Ball Position: Driver
body: Driver ball position is forward in stance, opposite the lead heel or instep. This allows the club to bottom out and catch the ball on the upswing (positive attack angle), maximizing launch and reducing spin. Checkpoint: tee height shows half the ball above the clubface crown. Too far back creates steep angle and high spin.

title: Ball Position: Irons
body: Iron ball position moves progressively back as clubs get shorter. Long irons: 1-2 balls inside lead heel. Mid irons: center-left of center. Short irons/wedges: center of stance. This matches each club's designed low point and promotes ball-first contact. Hitting thin? Ball may be too forward. Hitting fat? Ball may be too far back.

title: Face and Path: Ball Flight Laws
body: Ball starts where the face points and curves away from the path. Face is 75-85% responsible for start direction. Path determines curve. Example: face pointing right of target, path going more right = push draw. Understanding this helps diagnose misses. Slice = face open to path. Hook = face closed to path. Use this to work backward from ball flight to fix.

title: Clubface Control at Impact
body: Controlling the clubface is the most important impact factor. Face angle determines 75-85% of starting direction. Key influences: grip strength, forearm rotation, wrist angles. To close face: strengthen grip, feel trail hand rotating over lead. To open face: weaken grip, hold off release. Practice with impact tape to see face control patterns.

title: Swing Path Control
body: Club path is the direction the clubhead travels through impact (relative to target line). In-to-out path promotes draws; out-to-in promotes fades. Path is influenced by: stance alignment, shoulder turn, downswing sequence. To shallow path (more in-to-out): feel trail elbow drop, rotate hips first. To steepen path: feel hands move out toward ball.

title: Low Point Control
body: Low point is where the club reaches its lowest position in the swing arc. For irons, low point should be 2-4 inches ahead of the ball—this creates ball-first contact with descending blow. Fat shots: low point behind ball. Thin shots: low point at or past ball, or hitting up. Drill: place tee 4 inches ahead of ball, try to clip it after striking ball.

title: Center Face Contact
body: Strike location dramatically affects distance and direction. Center strikes maximize ball speed and minimize gear effect. Toe strikes lose distance and curve right (for right-handers). Heel strikes lose distance and curve left. Use foot spray or impact tape to check your pattern. Most amateurs strike toward the heel—stand slightly farther from ball to compensate.

title: Swing Tempo Fundamentals
body: Tempo is the overall pace of your swing—the ratio of backswing to downswing time. Tour average is 3:1 (backswing takes 3x longer than downswing). Consistent tempo improves timing and contact. Find your natural tempo: some players are quick (Nick Price), others smooth (Ernie Els). Key: whatever your tempo, keep it consistent shot to shot.

title: Tempo Drills and Training
body: To improve tempo: 1) Count 'one' on backswing, 'two' at top, 'three' through impact. 2) Swing to music with consistent BPM. 3) Practice with feet together to eliminate compensation. 4) Make slow-motion swings maintaining positions. Under pressure, tempo quickens—practice deliberately slow swings before important shots.

title: Kinematic Sequence: Proper Order
body: Efficient swings fire body segments in order: hips, torso, arms, club. The downswing should start from the ground up—hips rotate first while club is still going back. This creates separation and lag, storing energy for release. Common fault: starting down with arms/hands (casting). Feel: plant lead foot, rotate hips, let arms follow.

title: Weight Transfer Basics
body: Proper weight transfer shifts pressure from centered at address, to trail side in backswing (60-70%), then to lead side through impact (80-90%). Feel: load into trail hip going back, push off trail foot starting down. Common faults: reverse pivot (weight forward in backswing), hanging back (weight stays on trail side). Drill: step-through swings.

title: Slice: Causes and Fixes
body: A slice curves dramatically left-to-right (for right-handers), caused by face open to path. Main causes: weak grip, out-to-in path, early release, over-the-top move. Fixes: strengthen grip (see 3 knuckles), feel club dropping inside on downswing, close stance slightly. Quick fix: aim feet right and feel like you're swinging to right field.

title: Hook: Causes and Fixes
body: A hook curves dramatically right-to-left (for right-handers), caused by face closed to path. Main causes: too strong grip, excessive in-to-out path, over-rotation of hands. Fixes: weaken grip slightly, open stance, feel like hands stay quiet through impact. Check: if you're flipping hands aggressively at impact, that's often the culprit.

title: Push: Causes and Fixes
body: A push starts right of target and stays right (for right-handers), caused by face and path both pointing right. Main causes: ball too far back in stance, excessive in-to-out path with face matching path, sliding past the ball. Fixes: check ball position, feel more rotation through impact, ensure weight reaches lead side.

title: Pull: Causes and Fixes
body: A pull starts left of target and stays left (for right-handers), caused by face and path both pointing left. Main causes: ball too far forward, over-the-top path with face matching, early extension causing arms to swing left. Fixes: check ball position, feel trail elbow dropping on downswing, maintain posture through impact.

title: Thin Shots: Causes and Fixes
body: Thin shots contact the ball at or above its equator, resulting in low, running shots. Causes: early extension (standing up), ball too far forward, hanging back on trail side, looking up early. Fixes: maintain spine angle through impact, ensure weight shifts forward, keep eyes on ball through contact. Drill: hit balls with head against wall or partner's hand on head.

title: Fat Shots: Causes and Fixes
body: Fat shots hit the ground before the ball, resulting in short, weak shots. Causes: low point too far behind ball, weight staying back, excessive lateral sway, over-bending at knees through impact. Fixes: feel chest over ball at impact, shift weight to lead side, place tee 4 inches ahead and try to clip it. Ball position may be too far back.

title: Topped Shots: Causes and Fixes
body: Topped shots contact only the very top of the ball, resulting in worm-burners. Causes: lifting up during swing, straightening legs, ball too far forward, looking up too early. Different from thin: topped means contact above center. Fixes: maintain knee flex, keep spine angle, swing through to finish rather than at the ball.

title: Shank: Causes and Fixes
body: A shank contacts the hosel, sending ball sharply right (for right-handers). Terrifying but fixable. Causes: standing too close, hands moving outward in downswing, early extension pushing hips toward ball, weight moving to toes. Fixes: feel weight in heels, stand slightly farther away, make practice swings missing a headcover placed outside the ball.

title: Over the Top: Causes and Fixes
body: Over the top describes a downswing where the club moves outside the backswing plane, creating steep out-to-in path. Causes: starting downswing with shoulders/arms instead of lower body, tension, trying to hit hard. Fixes: feel trail elbow drop to hip, start downswing with hip bump/rotation, pause at top drill, slow-motion transitions.

title: Early Extension: The Posture Killer
body: Early extension means hips thrust toward ball during downswing, forcing you to stand up. This causes inconsistent contact (thins, fats, shanks) and loss of power. Causes: poor setup posture, inability to rotate hips while maintaining tilt, physical limitations. Fixes: feel backside moving away from ball on downswing, wall drill, hip mobility work.

title: Casting: Early Release Fix
body: Casting is releasing wrist angle too early in downswing, losing lag and power. Causes: hitting at ball instead of through it, tension, trying to help ball up. Fixes: feel like hands lead clubhead into impact, pump drill (stop at impact position), preset impact position drill. Focus on body rotation pulling arms through, not hands hitting at ball.

title: Sway: Lateral Movement Fix
body: Sway is excessive lateral movement (instead of rotation) in the backswing or downswing. Backswing sway moves head/body outside trail foot. Downswing sway slides without rotation. Both hurt contact and power. Fixes: feel rotation around spine axis, keep head relatively centered, use alignment stick behind trail hip to prevent backswing sway.

title: Reverse Pivot Fix
body: Reverse pivot means weight moves toward target in backswing and away in downswing—opposite of correct. Causes weak, inconsistent contact. Signs: leaning toward target at top of backswing, falling back at impact. Fixes: feel loading into trail hip going back, pushing off trail foot starting down. Drill: step-through swings exaggerating weight shift.

title: Chicken Wing: Lead Arm Breakdown
body: Chicken wing describes lead elbow bending and pointing outward through impact, losing extension and power. Causes: trying to lift ball, lack of body rotation, early extension. Fixes: feel lead arm and chest stay connected through impact, brush headcover under lead armpit through swing, focus on rotating body rather than arm manipulation.

title: Proper Wrist Hinge
body: Wrist hinge creates lag and stores power. Hinge should occur naturally during backswing—feel thumbs pointing up halfway back. Maintain hinge until lower body rotation pulls hands through impact. Common faults: no hinge (arms-only swing), too early unhinge (casting). The hinge angle should increase slightly in transition before releasing through impact.

title: Full Shoulder Turn
body: A complete shoulder turn creates width and power in your backswing. Goal: lead shoulder turns under chin, roughly 90 degrees from address. Feel: back faces target at top (if flexible enough). Maintain spine tilt while turning. Limited turn reduces power and forces arms to overwork. Flexibility limitations? Make fullest comfortable turn, don't force.

title: Hip Turn and Restriction
body: Hips turn about half as much as shoulders in backswing (45 degrees vs 90), creating torque between upper and lower body. This X-factor stores energy for downswing. Too much hip turn loses power; too little creates strain. Feel: trail hip turns and loads weight while maintaining knee flex. Lead knee can move inward slightly but avoid excessive slide.

title: Arms and Body Connection
body: Connection means arms and body work together, not independently. Feel: upper arms maintain light contact with chest through swing. Glove or towel under lead armpit drill reinforces this. Connected swings are more consistent because body rotation controls arm movement. Disconnection causes timing issues—arms racing ahead or lagging behind body.

title: Balanced Finish Position
body: A balanced finish indicates a good swing. Checkpoints: weight fully on lead foot, belt buckle facing target, chest facing slightly left of target, club behind head or over lead shoulder, able to hold finish for 3+ seconds. If you're falling backward or forward, something earlier in swing is off. Use finish as diagnostic tool.

title: Pre-Shot Routine Basics
body: A consistent pre-shot routine improves focus and reduces tension. Elements: stand behind ball to pick target line, take practice swing(s), address ball with specific checkpoints, one look at target, swing. Keep it under 20-25 seconds. The routine should be automatic—same every time. Under pressure, trust the routine and commit fully.

title: Visualization and Commitment
body: Visualize your shot before swinging: see the ball flight, landing spot, and result. This programs your brain and body for the task. Commit 100% to your chosen shot—doubt causes tension and poor swings. If you can't commit, step back and reconsider. Half-hearted swings rarely produce good results. Trust your preparation and let it go.

title: Breathing for Golf
body: Proper breathing reduces tension and improves focus. Exhale during downswing—holding breath creates tension. Take a deep breath during pre-shot routine to calm nerves. If feeling anxious, use box breathing: 4 counts in, 4 counts hold, 4 counts out, 4 counts hold. Relaxed muscles move faster and more fluidly than tense ones.

title: Eliminating Tension
body: Tension is the swing killer. Signs: tight grip, raised shoulders, locked jaw, holding breath. Causes: trying too hard, fear of outcome, mechanical thoughts. Fixes: waggle club before swing, consciously relax shoulders, grip lighter, focus on target not mechanics, accept that bad shots happen. Your practice swing is usually more relaxed—replicate that feel.

title: Focus and Target Orientation
body: During the swing, focus externally (target, ball flight) not internally (body positions). Internal focus during execution causes paralysis by analysis. Save mechanical thoughts for practice. On course, pick a small target and let your trained body execute. If you must think of something, make it one simple feel, not a checklist.

title: Practice Mode vs Play Mode
body: Practice mode: work on mechanics, try new things, embrace failures. Play mode: trust what you have, commit to targets, accept results. Mixing these hurts both. On the course, you play with the swing you brought that day. If it's not working, focus on course management rather than mid-round swing changes.

title: Recovering from Bad Shots
body: Bad shots happen to everyone. Key is limiting damage—don't follow a bad shot with a worse one trying to recover. Mental reset: walk to ball, take deep breaths, assess next shot fresh without carrying frustration. Physical reset: shadow swing to feel good mechanics. Accept the result, make the best decision for next shot, move on.

title: Effective Swing Thoughts
body: Limit swing thoughts to one per shot. Too many thoughts cause paralysis. Effective thoughts are simple and feel-based: 'smooth tempo', 'rotate through', 'finish balanced'. Avoid positions ('keep elbow here')—these are for practice. Find a thought that works and stick with it that day. Change only if something stops working over multiple holes.

title: Pre-Round Warmup Routine
body: Arrive 30-45 minutes before tee time. Start with stretching: hip circles, arm swings, torso rotations. On range: begin with wedges, work up through irons to driver, then back down. Focus on tempo and contact, not distance. Hit some shots with your typical ball flight shape. End with your first tee club. On green: lag putts for speed, then short putts for confidence.

title: Golf-Specific Stretches
body: Key stretches for golf: hip flexors (lunge stretch), thoracic spine (rotation while seated), hamstrings (toe touch), shoulders (cross-body and overhead). Hold each 15-30 seconds, no bouncing. Dynamic stretches before play (movement-based), static stretches after. Even 5 minutes prevents injury and improves turn. Tight hips especially limit swing power and cause compensations.

title: Playing in Rain
body: Rain changes everything: grips get slick, ball doesn't fly as far, greens slow down. Adjustments: use rain gloves or keep towel handy, grip lighter to prevent slipping, take more club (wet ball flies shorter), expect less roll on wet fairways, play for more break on greens (balls don't release as much). Keep grips and ball dry between shots.

title: Wind: Basic Adjustments
body: Into wind: take more club, swing easier (hard swings add spin, ball balloons), play ball slightly back to lower flight. Downwind: less club, normal swing, accept extra roll. Crosswind: aim into it and let it bring ball back, or curve ball into wind to straighten flight. Key: don't fight the wind—use it strategically.

title: Driver: Purpose and Design
body: The driver is designed for maximum distance off the tee on long holes. Longest shaft, lowest loft (8-12 degrees typically), largest head (460cc max). Hit off a tee to allow ascending blow (positive attack angle). Not for every hole—use when fairway width and lack of hazards allow for driver's larger dispersion. When accuracy matters more, consider fairway wood or hybrid.

title: Driver Loft Selection
body: More loft generally helps most amateurs. Lower loft (8-9°) suits high swing speeds with low spin. Higher loft (10.5-12°) helps slower swingers launch higher for more carry. Signs you need more loft: low ball flight, excessive spin, hitting down on ball. Signs you need less: balloon flight, too much spin from high launch. Get fitted or test multiple lofts.

title: Fairway Woods: 3-Wood and 5-Wood
body: Fairway woods offer distance from fairway or tee when driver is too risky. 3-wood (13-15°): longest fairway option, can be difficult to hit from tight lies. 5-wood (18-19°): easier to launch, versatile for fairway and rough. Hit with sweeping motion, ball positioned forward of center. Useful for long par 5 layups and reachable par 4 tees where accuracy matters.

title: Hybrids: The Versatile Option
body: Hybrids combine fairway wood forgiveness with iron-like control. Replace hard-to-hit long irons (3-4 iron). Benefits: higher launch from rough, more forgiving on mishits, versatile from many lies. Setup: play like a mid-iron (ball center-forward), swing like an iron (descending blow). Great for long approaches, tee shots on tight holes, and recovery from rough.

title: Long Irons: When to Use
body: Long irons (2-4 iron) offer lower flight and more control than hybrids but require solid contact. Better players choose long irons for: penetrating flight in wind, controlled tee shots, running approach shots. Setup: ball forward of center, weight slightly favoring lead side. These are the hardest clubs to hit—most amateurs benefit from replacing with hybrids.

title: Mid Irons: The Scoring Zone
body: Mid irons (5-7 iron) are your approach club workhorses from 140-180 yards. Designed for consistent distance and trajectory. Ball position: center to slightly forward. Focus on clean contact—these should be among your most reliable clubs. Practice different trajectories: normal, knockdown, high soft. Most approach shots should be hit with mid irons when possible.

title: Short Irons: Precision Clubs
body: Short irons (8-9 iron) and pitching wedge are precision clubs for 100-140 yards. Higher loft means more spin and stopping power. Ball position: center of stance. These should be your most accurate clubs—if you're struggling with short irons, your swing has fundamental issues. Practice distance control: know your carry number to each landing spot.

title: Wedges: Your Scoring Arsenal
body: Wedges control the short game: pitching wedge (44-48°), gap wedge (50-52°), sand wedge (54-56°), lob wedge (58-60°). Each serves different distances and trajectories. Carry gaps should be 10-15 yards between wedges. Know your carry distance with each wedge at full, 3/4, and 1/2 swings. Wedge practice has highest ROI for scoring improvement.

title: Gap Wedge: Filling the Distance Gap
body: Gap wedge (50-52°) bridges the distance between pitching wedge and sand wedge. Essential for full shots in the 90-110 yard range where PW is too much and SW too little. Also useful for longer pitch shots. If you have a yardage dead zone, you likely need a gap wedge. Carry all four wedges if your bag allows.

title: Sand Wedge: Not Just for Bunkers
body: Sand wedge (54-56°) is versatile: bunker shots, pitch shots, chips around green. Higher bounce (10-14°) helps in soft sand and fluffy lies; prevents digging. Full swing distance typically 80-100 yards. Practice different swing lengths to dial in your distances. Don't reserve it only for bunkers—it's often the best choice for standard pitch shots.

title: Lob Wedge: High Risk, High Reward
body: Lob wedge (58-60°) is for high, soft shots that stop quickly: short-sided pins, over bunkers, tight lies needing height. Requires precise contact—thin and fat shots are magnified. Not for everyone: many pros don't carry one. If you use it, practice extensively. Alternative: open your sand wedge face for similar effect with more forgiveness.

title: Putter Selection Basics
body: Putter is the most used club—40%+ of strokes for most golfers. Key factors: head shape (blade vs mallet), toe hang (matches stroke arc), length (eyes over ball), weight (personal preference). Mallet putters offer more forgiveness; blades offer more feel. Get fitted or test multiple styles. Most important: confidence and consistency.

title: Club Gapping Fundamentals
body: Proper gapping means consistent yardage intervals between clubs. Goal: 10-15 yard gaps with no dead zones. Common issue: big gap between PW and SW (20+ yards). Solution: add gap wedge. To check gapping: hit 10 balls with each club, record carry distances, identify gaps. Consider hybrid to replace hard-to-hit long irons if there's a gap at the top.

title: Wedge Distance Matrix
body: Build your wedge matrix: for each wedge, know carry distance at full, 3/4, 1/2, and 1/4 swings. Example matrix: PW full=130, 3/4=115, 1/2=95. SW full=95, 3/4=80, 1/2=65. This gives you multiple options for each distance. Practice on range with targets. On course, pick the swing that matches your distance needs.

title: Tee Club Selection Strategy
body: Driver isn't always the answer. Consider: fairway width, hazard positions, your miss pattern, hole length. On tight holes or when hazards lurk at driver distance, club down to 3-wood, hybrid, or even iron. The goal is hitting the fairway at a distance that leaves a comfortable approach. Laying back to your favorite yardage often beats driver in rough.

title: Club Selection from Fairway
body: From a clean fairway lie, you can hit any club in your bag. Choose based on distance needed and conditions. Factors: wind direction, pin position, miss consequences. If between clubs, consider: uphill approach needs more club, downhill less; into wind add 1-2 clubs; downwind subtract. When in doubt, take the longer club and swing easier for control.

title: Club Selection from Rough
body: Rough reduces distance and control. Light rough: lose 5-10%, can still hit most clubs. Heavy rough: lose 15-25%, avoid long irons/woods—use hybrids or take a wedge and advance. Consider lie: ball sitting up is easier than nestled down. Flyer lies (light rough, grass behind ball) can add distance unpredictably—club down 5-10 yards. Always prioritize getting out.

title: Downhill Lie Club Selection
body: On a downhill lie, the effective loft decreases (ball launches lower). Take 1-2 more clubs than usual distance. Ball tends to curve more (often fade for righties). Setup: match shoulders to slope, play ball slightly back, weight favors lower foot. Make a controlled swing—full swings are difficult to balance. Aim for safe side; mishits are common.

title: Uphill Lie Club Selection
body: On an uphill lie, effective loft increases (ball launches higher). Take 1-2 less clubs than usual distance. Ball tends to draw more for right-handers. Setup: match shoulders to slope, ball position slightly forward, weight may feel in lower foot. The hill helps you get the ball up, so lower-lofted clubs become easier to hit. Expect more draw/hook curvature.

title: Ball Above Feet: Club Selection
body: When ball is above your feet, it naturally wants to curve right-to-left (hook for righties). Club effects: grip down to compensate for being closer to ball, aim right of target to allow for draw. Take one less club (ball tends to go farther due to de-lofting effect of lie). Maintain balance throughout swing.

title: Ball Below Feet: Club Selection
body: When ball is below your feet, it naturally wants to curve left-to-right (fade for righties). Club effects: maintain knee flex throughout swing, aim left of target to allow for fade. May need one more club due to added loft effect. This is a difficult lie—prioritize solid contact over distance. Consider playing to center of green.

title: Punch Shot Club Selection
body: Punch shots are low, controlled shots under trees or into wind. Club selection: mid-iron (5-7 iron) with ball back in stance. Grip down for control. Make 3/4 swing with abbreviated follow-through. The ball runs more than normal—account for rollout. Useful for recovery and wind. Practice this shot—it saves strokes when needed.

title: Flighted Wedge Shots
body: A flighted wedge is a lower-trajectory wedge shot for control in wind or when needing to run the ball. Use gap or sand wedge, ball slightly back, hands ahead, 3/4 swing with low finish. Produces less spin and more roll. Useful for: into-wind approaches, firm greens, back pins with room to run. Practice the distance it carries vs total.

title: High Soft Landing Shots
body: High soft shots land gently with minimal roll for tight pins or over hazards. Use lob or sand wedge with face slightly open. Ball forward, full swing with high finish. More spin means less roll. Risk: thin shots go low and far; fat shots come up short. Only use when necessary—it's higher risk. Standard trajectory is usually preferred.

title: Bump and Run Club Selection
body: Bump and run is a low chip that rolls to the hole like a putt. Use less-lofted club (7-9 iron) for more roll, more-lofted (PW-GW) for less roll. Calculate: land ball on first third, let it roll two-thirds. Safer than high lofted chips—less can go wrong. Ideal when no hazards between you and pin, and green allows rolling approach.

title: When to Chip vs Pitch
body: Chip: low shot that rolls most of its distance. Use when: no obstacles, room to land on green, want predictability. Pitch: higher shot that carries most of its distance. Use when: obstacle to carry, limited green to work with, need to stop quickly. Default to chipping when possible—it's more consistent. Pitch only when necessary.

title: Club Selection Adjustments for Wind
body: Into wind: add 1 club per 10mph of wind, consider 2 clubs for strong gusts. Ball flight is exaggerated—slice becomes bigger slice. Swing easier to reduce spin (high spin balloons in wind). Downwind: subtract club, expect more roll. Crosswind: aim into it or play a curve that uses the wind. In strong wind, prioritize control over distance.

title: Club Selection for Elevation Changes
body: Uphill approach: add 1 club per 10 yards of elevation rise—ball must climb, using more energy. Downhill approach: subtract 1 club per 10 yards drop—ball has farther to fall. Mountain courses amplify these effects. Also consider ball flies farther at altitude due to thinner air—roughly 2% per 1000ft above sea level.

title: First Tee Club Selection
body: First hole jitters make the opening tee shot challenging. Strategy: hit the club you're most confident with, even if it's not driver. A smooth 3-wood or hybrid in the fairway beats a stressed driver in the rough. Warm up with your first-tee club last. Make your simplest swing. The goal is starting well, not showing off distance.

title: Layup Club Selection
body: On par 5s or long par 4s, layup to your favorite full-swing wedge distance. Most players: 80-100 yards. Calculate backward from green: if 100 yards is your number and green is 350 yards from your drive landing spot, hit club that goes 250 yards. Avoid leaving awkward half-wedge distances. A full swing from your yardage beats a tricky partial shot.

title: Recovery Shot Club Selection
body: In trouble (trees, rough, difficult lies), priority is escaping safely. Take your medicine: pick a conservative club that guarantees back in play. A sideways 7-iron to the fairway beats a heroic 3-wood into more trouble. Calculate: what's the lowest-risk shot that advances the ball meaningfully? One penalty stroke is better than two from compounding errors.

title: Club Loft: What It Means
body: Loft is the angle of the clubface relative to vertical. Higher loft = higher launch, more spin, shorter distance. Driver: 8-12°, pitching wedge: 44-48°, lob wedge: 58-60°. Modern clubs have strengthened lofts (lower than traditional) for marketing distance. Your 7-iron might have 5-iron loft from decades ago. Know your actual lofts for proper gapping.

title: Lie Angle Explained
body: Lie angle is the angle between the shaft and ground at address. Too upright (toe up at impact): shots go left. Too flat (heel up at impact): shots go right. Proper lie has sole flush to ground at impact. Fitting determines correct lie for your height and swing. Standard clubs may not fit you—custom lie adjustment improves accuracy significantly.

title: Shaft Flex Selection
body: Shaft flex affects timing and trajectory. Too stiff: low ball flight, shots tend right (face open at impact). Too soft: high flight, shots tend left (face closes early). General guidelines by swing speed: <75mph=Ladies, 75-85=Senior, 85-95=Regular, 95-105=Stiff, 105+=X-Stiff. Get fit using launch monitor—feel alone isn't reliable.

title: Shaft Weight Effects
body: Heavier shafts: more control, potentially slower swing speed. Lighter shafts: faster swing speed, less control. Iron shafts: steel (heavier, 90-130g) for control, graphite (lighter, 50-80g) for speed and vibration dampening. Seniors and those seeking distance often benefit from graphite. Better players often prefer steel for control. Match weight to your needs.

title: Swing Weight Feel
body: Swing weight measures how heavy the club feels during swing (head weight vs grip weight). Scale: C0-D9 typically, with D2 being common for men's clubs. Higher swing weight = clubhead feels heavier. Affects tempo and timing. Consistent swing weight across set creates consistent feel. Adding lead tape to head increases swing weight; heavier grip decreases it.

title: Club Length Effects
body: Longer clubs: more potential speed (longer lever) but harder to control. Shorter clubs: more control but less speed. Standard lengths are just averages—fitting optimizes for your height, arm length, and swing. Many amateurs benefit from slightly shorter clubs for better contact. Driver length has increased over years; many struggle with 45.5+ inch drivers.

title: Launch and Spin Windows
body: Optimal launch and spin maximize carry distance. Driver ideal: 12-15° launch, 2000-2500 rpm spin (varies by speed). Too high spin with high launch = balloon. Too low spin with low launch = nose dive. Irons: higher launch, more spin for stopping power. Launch monitors help dial in—fitting optimizes these for your swing speed and attack angle.

title: Gear Effect: Off-Center Hits
body: Gear effect causes sidespin on off-center hits due to clubhead twisting. Toe hits produce draw spin (curves left for righties). Heel hits produce fade spin (curves right). Modern drivers with MOI design reduce this effect but don't eliminate it. Understanding gear effect explains why mishits curve. Center contact minimizes gear effect.

title: Driver Tee Height
body: Optimal tee height shows half the ball above the clubface crown at address. Too low: steep strike, high spin, lost distance. Too high: sky marks, inconsistent contact. Adjust for conditions: lower in wind for reduced spin, standard height normally. Consistent tee height promotes consistent contact. Find your optimal and replicate it every time.

title: Driver Attack Angle
body: Attack angle is the vertical direction of clubhead movement at impact. For driver, positive (upward) attack angle optimizes launch and reduces spin. Typical range: +2° to +5° is ideal. Hitting down on driver increases spin dramatically, costing distance. Ball forward in stance and spine tilt away from target promote upward strike.

title: Driver Face Strike Patterns
body: Strike location dramatically affects driver performance. Center: max ball speed, optimal launch. High-center: lower spin, higher launch (often ideal). Low: higher spin, lower launch. Toe: gear effect draw, lost speed. Heel: gear effect fade, lost speed. Use impact tape or foot spray to identify your pattern. Most miss low-heel; tee higher or stand farther.

title: Wedge Bounce Explained
body: Bounce is the angle between leading edge and lowest point of sole. High bounce (12-14°): prevents digging, great for soft conditions and fluffy sand. Low bounce (4-8°): allows versatility on tight lies and firm conditions, more digging risk. Mid bounce (8-12°): all-around option. Match bounce to your typical conditions and swing style (steep diggers need more bounce).

title: Wedge Grind Options
body: Grind is the shaping of the sole to improve turf interaction. Full sole (no grind): most forgiveness, best for firm conditions from square face. Heel grind: allows face opening for flop shots. Toe grind: helps from tight lies. M-grind/S-grind etc.: manufacturer-specific all-purpose grinds. Match to your short game style and course conditions.

title: Wedge Selection by Conditions
body: Soft conditions (wet grass, fluffy sand): use higher bounce to prevent digging, fuller sole. Firm conditions (hard pan, tight lies, packed sand): use lower bounce, heel/toe relief to allow clean contact. If you play one course mostly, optimize for those conditions. If you travel, carry wedges suited to different conditions or pick mid-bounce versatility.

title: Putter Toe Hang and Stroke
body: Toe hang indicates how much the toe drops when balanced on your finger. High toe hang: for arcing strokes (face opens going back, closes through). Face-balanced (no toe hang): for straight-back-straight-through strokes. Quarter toe hang: for slight arc. Match putter to your natural stroke. Mismatched putters fight your natural motion and cause pushes/pulls.

title: Putter Length Fitting
body: Proper putter length allows eyes directly over ball with arms hanging naturally. Too long: eyes outside ball, pushes. Too short: hunching over, cramped stroke. Standard is 33-35 inches, but custom fitting is crucial. At address: forearms should hang perpendicular to ground or slightly angled. Grip end shouldn't rest against forearm (too long) or require reaching (too short).

title: Golf Ball Selection Basics
body: Golf balls vary in construction and feel. Two-piece (distance balls): firmer, less spin, more durable, best for beginners and high handicaps. Multi-layer (tour balls): softer feel, more spin control, better for skilled players. Spin: low-spin balls reduce hooks/slices but offer less stopping power. Match ball to your game—most amateurs don't need tour balls.

title: Why Club Fitting Matters
body: Properly fit clubs improve consistency and maximize your potential. Fitting optimizes: length, lie, loft, shaft flex/weight, grip size. Even beginners benefit from basic fitting. Off-the-rack clubs are built for average body—you're likely not average. A $500 fitted set often outperforms $1500 wrong-fit premium clubs. Get fit before major purchases.

title: Grip Size Effects
body: Grip size affects hand action and shot shape. Undersized grips: promote hand action, can cause hooks. Oversized grips: quiet hands, can cause fades/blocks. Standard sizing: measure from crease at wrist to middle fingertip. Most common fit: standard or midsize. Arthritis or large hands may need jumbo. Consistent grips across set for uniform feel.

title: Iron Head Design: Blades vs Cavity
body: Blade irons: smaller head, thin top line, minimal forgiveness, maximum workability. For skilled players. Cavity back: larger head, perimeter weighting, more forgiveness on mishits. Game improvement: largest head, most forgiveness, offset, thicker sole. Choose based on skill, not ego. Most amateurs hit cavity backs better. Better players may prefer player's cavities over pure blades.

title: Club Offset Explained
body: Offset positions clubface behind the hosel, giving hands extra time to square the face before impact. More offset = more help squaring face, fights slice. Less offset = more workability, preferred by better players. High-handicappers and slicers benefit from offset. As you improve, you may prefer less offset. Check your current clubs for offset amount.

title: Aim for the Safe Side
body: High-percentage approach strategy: aim where your worst miss is least penalized. Trouble right? Aim left-center so a push stays on green. This doesn't mean aiming at hazards—it means your target eliminates one side's danger. Use your typical miss pattern, not your perfect shot, to select targets. The pin isn't always the correct target.

title: Understanding Your Dispersion
body: Dispersion is your shot pattern—how widely shots scatter around your aim point. Know your dispersion: most amateurs have 30-40 yard spread with mid-irons. Plan targets assuming the full pattern, not the perfect shot. If your dispersion covers a hazard when aimed at the pin, move your target. Course management starts with honest self-assessment.

title: Center of Green Strategy
body: Aiming at flags is often a mistake. Strategy: aim at center of green, especially when pin is tucked near trouble. Results: more greens hit, fewer disasters, consistent proximity. A 30-footer from center beats a chip from bunker. Exception: short clubs (wedges) where you can attack. For mid/long irons, center green is the percentage play.

title: Risk/Reward Decision Making
body: Before aggressive plays, calculate: What do I gain if it works? What do I lose if it fails? Expected value = (success rate × gain) - (failure rate × penalty). Example: going for par-5 in two gives birdie chance 30% but brings water into play 40% of time. Laying up to wedge range might have higher expected strokes. Play the percentages.

title: Tee Shot Strategy
body: Tee strategy isn't always 'hit driver far'. Consider: Where do I want my approach from? What miss can I afford? Where's the trouble? Pick a club that eliminates the dangerous miss while leaving a manageable approach. Sometimes 3-wood to the wide part of fairway beats driver flirting with hazards. Play to your strengths.

title: Miss Management
body: Everyone misses—strategy is controlling where misses go. Before each shot, identify the acceptable miss (usually short and safe side of target). Pick club and target that make your likely miss acceptable. Example: if you typically fade, aim at left-center; your miss fades to middle, your good shot is left-center. Eliminate disasters.

title: Playing Around Hazards
body: Hazards (water, bunkers, OB) require strategic thought. Calculate: can I clear it with my typical shot, not my best? If no, lay up. If yes, how much margin? Aim away from hazard to build in miss room. For forced carries, take enough club to clear even on a slight mishit. Penalty strokes from hazards destroy scores faster than lost distance.

title: Par 5 Strategy
body: Par 5s are birdie opportunities when played smart. Two approaches: 1) Go for it in two if risk is low and you have the distance. 2) Lay up to your favorite wedge distance for a makeable birdie putt. Avoid leaving awkward third shot distances. Three solid shots often beats two great shots and a disaster. Know your strengths.

title: Layup Yardage Selection
body: When laying up, don't just 'hit it close'—lay up to a specific yardage. Most players have a favorite wedge distance (80-100 yards). Calculate backward: if you want 90 yards left and the green is 250 yards away, you need to hit 160 yards. Avoid half-wedge distances (50-60 yards)—most amateurs struggle there. Full swings are more consistent.

title: Avoiding Awkward Distances
body: Half-swing wedges (40-60 yards) are among the hardest shots in golf. Strategy: lay up or go for it to avoid them. On par 5s, calculate to leave full wedge. On par 4s where driver leaves awkward distance, consider teeing 3-wood to leave better number. Full confident swings beat tentative half-swings. Know your comfortable wedge distances.

title: Short Game Decision Framework
body: Around the green, pick the safest shot that gets the job done. Decision order: 1) Can I putt? If yes, putt. 2) Can I chip (low running shot)? If yes, chip. 3) Must I pitch? Only pitch if obstacles demand it. Putting is safest, then chipping, then pitching. Higher shots have more variables. Keep it simple.

title: Chip Shot Landing Spot
body: For chips, pick a landing spot, not just a target. Formula: land ball one-third of the way, let it roll two-thirds. Adjust for slope and speed. Uphill: land shorter, ball will release less. Downhill: more carry needed or use less loft. Visualize the ball landing and rolling to the hole like a putt. Practice this read on the practice green.

title: Pitch Shot Landing Strategy
body: Pitch shots (higher trajectory) carry further and roll less. Pick a landing spot that accounts for one hop and check. Usually land pitch 3-6 feet short of target area. On firm greens, land shorter and allow release. On soft greens, you can be more aggressive. Practice pitch shots to learn how your ball reacts on different landing spots.

title: Bunker Shot Strategy
body: From greenside bunkers, goal is getting out in one and on the green—not getting close. Assess: lie, sand firmness, lip height, pin position. Buried lie = lower expectations (just get out). Good lie = can be aggressive at pin. Always clear the lip with margin. Two-putt from the green beats another bunker shot. Conservative targets from bad lies.

title: Putting Strategy Overview
body: Putting strategy prioritizes avoiding three-putts over making every putt. For long putts: focus on speed, get ball in 3-foot circle. For mid-range: proper read, confident stroke. For short putts: pick line, commit, execute. More strokes are lost to three-putts than gained from made long putts. Lag putting is the most important putting skill.

title: Lag Putting: Speed Control
body: Lag putting gets long putts close enough to avoid three-putts. Focus: speed over line. For 30+ footers, distance judgment matters more than perfect read. Drill: practice to a 3-foot circle instead of the hole. Mental approach: 'roll the ball dead weight' to stop near hole regardless of break. The goal is two putts, not one putt.

title: Uphill Putt Strategy
body: Uphill putts are easier—they don't get away from you. Strategy: be aggressive. Aim to get ball to the hole; even a slight miss finishes close. Can play less break than it appears because slower pace holds line better. On short uphill putts, commit and roll it firmly. These are the most makeable putts on the green.

title: Downhill Putt Strategy
body: Downhill putts are dangerous—they can get away quickly. Strategy: conservative pace. Aim to die the ball at the hole; too firm races past. Play more break than it appears because slow pace allows ball to fall. For very fast downhillers, consider putting to a spot short of the hole and letting gravity bring it in. Three-putt avoidance is priority.

title: Reading Break: Basic Principles
body: Putts break toward lower ground. Read from behind ball and behind hole. Consider: overall slope, grain direction (subtle effect), speed (faster = less break, slower = more break). For big breakers, aim at the apex—the highest point of the curve—and trust gravity. Most amateurs under-read and under-commit. When in doubt, play more break.

title: Green Reading Method
body: Effective green reading uses feet and eyes. Walk the putt line feeling slope with your feet. Dominant slope usually determines break. Use lowest point around the hole as guide—ball will break toward it. Grain follows drainage (ball breaks toward valley/water). Shadows can help see slope. Trust your first read; second-guessing causes tentative strokes.

title: Pin Position Response
body: Pin positions determine aggression level. Front pins: easier to attack, can land short and roll to hole. Middle pins: standard aim at center. Back pins: most difficult, consider leaving below hole, avoid going long. Tucked pins (near edge/trouble): often best to ignore pin and aim at center. The pin doesn't always warrant attention.

title: Below the Hole Strategy
body: Leaving your ball below the hole (uphill next putt) is a core strategy. Uphill putts are easier: more aggressive speed, more forgiving, no fear of racing past. Plan approaches to leave below hole, even if farther from pin. Three-putt from above the hole happens often; from below, rarely. Sacrifice proximity for position.

title: Taking Enough Club
body: Most amateurs come up short. Solution: when between clubs, take more club. Club up and swing easier for control. Front of green is often not where the trouble is—back or sides hold hazards. Exception: severe back-to-front slope where long means downhill nightmare. Default: take the extra club. Your ego doesn't need driver distance; your scorecard needs greens hit.

title: Wind Strategy
body: Wind changes everything. Into wind: take extra clubs, swing smooth to reduce spin, expect less curve. Downwind: take less club, expect more roll, expect curve to be magnified. Crosswind: aim into wind and let it bring ball back, or curve into wind for straight flight. Strong wind: play conservative targets, prioritize fairways and centers of greens.

title: Scoring Zone Improvement
body: Scoring zone is inside 100 yards. This is where handicaps are made or lost. Improvement priorities: 1) Lag putting to avoid three-putts, 2) Wedge distance control for proximity, 3) Chipping to save pars, 4) Short putt confidence. Most practice time should be in scoring zone—driving range bombs feel good but don't lower scores as much.

title: Course Management Mindset
body: Course management is playing smart golf. Accept your current skill level; play shots you can hit, not shots you've seen on TV. Conservative strategy: aim for fat parts of fairways, center of greens, avoid short-sided positions. Aggressive strategy only when: lie is good, target is reachable, penalty for miss is acceptable. Default to conservative.

title: Breaking 90: Bogey Golf Strategy
body: To break 90, target bogey on every hole (that's 18 over = 90). Strategy: eliminate double bogeys and worse. How: play for the middle of fairways/greens, don't compound errors, two-putt is fine. Every time you're in trouble, take safest route back to play. One bad shot doesn't have to become three. Manage mistakes; don't try to be heroic.

title: Breaking 80: Consistent Execution
body: To break 80, need to make some pars while limiting big numbers. Strategy: hit more greens in regulation, save par when you miss, capitalize on scoring holes (par 5s, short par 4s). Track stats: GIR, up-and-down percentage, three-putt rate. Improve weakest area. Mental: stay patient, one bad hole doesn't ruin a round. Think birdie on easy holes, par everywhere else.

title: Watching Playing Partners
body: Learn from others' shots. Watch their ball flight to see wind effects, green speed, break direction. If partner's putt breaks left, yours probably will too. If their approach releases 20 feet, factor that into your landing. Observe their good lies and bad lies to inform your targets. Smart observation is free course knowledge.

title: Playing an Unfamiliar Course
body: On unfamiliar courses, play conservative until you learn the layout. First time playing: aim for centers, note where trouble hides, watch how greens react. Don't assume you know how holes play—many have hidden hazards. If GPS/rangefinder allowed, use it heavily. Ask locals or starter about tricky holes. Second round on same course yields much better scores.

title: Out of Bounds vs Penalty Area
body: Out of bounds (OB, marked by white stakes) requires stroke-and-distance: add one penalty stroke and play again from previous spot. Penalty areas (yellow or red stakes) offer relief options near where ball crossed the margin with one-stroke penalty. OB is far more punitive—plan targets to keep misses away from OB lines. Red penalty areas offer lateral relief option.

title: Lost Ball Procedure
body: If you can't find your ball within 3 minutes of searching, it's lost. Penalty: stroke and distance—add one stroke and play from where you hit the previous shot. If you think a ball might be lost, play a provisional ball before searching. This saves time if original is lost. Without provisional, you must return to previous spot—pace of play killer.

title: Provisional Ball: When and How
body: Hit a provisional when ball might be OB or lost (not in penalty area). Announce 'I'm hitting a provisional' before hitting. Play provisional until you reach area of original. If original is found in bounds, pick up provisional and continue with original (no penalty). If original is lost/OB, provisional becomes ball in play (stroke + distance penalty already applied).

title: Unplayable Lie Options
body: You can declare ball unplayable anywhere except penalty areas. One-stroke penalty, then choose: 1) Return to previous spot (stroke and distance), 2) Drop within two club-lengths, not nearer hole, 3) Drop on line between hole and ball, going back as far as you want. In bunker: options 1&2 stay in bunker; option 3 can be outside for two-stroke penalty.

title: Embedded Ball Relief
body: If your ball is embedded in the general area (fairway, rough—not bunker or penalty area), you get free relief. Procedure: mark ball, lift, clean, drop within one club-length of where ball was embedded, not nearer the hole. Ball must be in its own pitch mark to be embedded. This rule applies in the general area unless course prohibits it.

title: Cart Path Relief
body: Free relief from cart paths and other artificial obstructions. Find nearest point of complete relief (stance and swing not on path), no nearer hole. Drop within one club-length of that point. You cannot choose which side of path to drop; must use nearest point. You can decline relief and play from path if you prefer.

title: Ground Under Repair (GUR)
body: Ground under repair (marked by white lines, GUR signs, or blue stakes) gives free relief. Procedure: find nearest point where ball and stance are outside GUR, not nearer hole. Drop within one club-length. If ball lies in GUR but you have good stance outside it, you still can take relief if GUR interferes with stroke.

title: Temporary Water Relief
body: Temporary water (puddles, large wet areas) provides free relief. For relief: water must be visible before or after taking stance. Find nearest point of complete relief (ball and stance clear of water), not nearer hole. Drop within one club-length. On putting green: place ball at nearest point of relief, can be off green if necessary.

title: Penalty Area Relief Options
body: Ball in penalty area (yellow or red stakes): options with one-stroke penalty. 1) Play as it lies (no penalty). 2) Stroke-and-distance (return to previous spot). 3) Back-on-the-line (drop on line from hole through crossing point). Yellow areas: options 1-3. Red areas: add option 4) Lateral relief within two club-lengths of crossing point, not nearer hole.

title: Bunker Rules Basics
body: In bunkers, you cannot touch sand with club before stroke (testing condition). Removing loose impediments (leaves, stones) is allowed. Ball embedded in bunker: no free relief (different from general area). Unplayable in bunker: lateral and back-on-line drops must stay in bunker; to drop outside bunker costs two strokes. Don't ground club at address.

title: Putting Green Rules
body: On the green, you may: mark, lift, and clean your ball; repair pitch marks and old hole plugs; remove loose impediments. You cannot: repair spike marks (unless damage caused by ball). Ball moved accidentally on green: replace with no penalty. Ball moved by wind: play from new spot. Flag stick may be left in or removed—no penalty if ball hits it.

title: Marking Your Ball
body: Mark ball when lifting on the green or when permitted elsewhere. Place marker directly behind ball (or to side if behind interferes with another player). Lift ball. When replacing, put ball directly in front of marker, then remove marker. If ball moves during marking/replacing, replace without penalty. Don't use a marker that could help with alignment.

title: Proper Dropping Procedure
body: When taking relief: mark original spot if needed. Determine relief area (usually one or two club-lengths). Stand outside relief area, hold ball at knee height, drop straight down. Ball must come to rest in relief area. If it rolls out, re-drop. If it rolls out again, place at spot where it touched ground on second drop. Club-lengths measured with longest club except putter.

title: Order of Play
body: Traditional: farthest from hole plays first. On tee: honors (lowest score on previous hole) plays first. Ready golf is encouraged for pace: anyone who's ready may play if safe. You can ask to play out of turn to maintain pace. In match play, playing out of turn can be recalled by opponent. Always be aware of others' positions for safety.

title: Ready Golf for Pace
body: Ready golf means playing when ready rather than strict order. Guidelines: tee off when ready if those ahead are safe, play approach when clear, putt out if convenient. Don't delay searching for ball while others wait. Keep pre-shot routine brief. Position yourself to play quickly when it's your turn. Goal: 4-hour rounds for most courses.

title: Repairing Pitch Marks
body: Always repair your pitch marks on greens. Technique: insert repair tool at edges of mark, push toward center from multiple angles, tamp down with putter. Do NOT lift center up—this damages roots. Repair one extra mark beyond yours; greens improve for everyone. Failing to repair is poor etiquette. Well-repaired marks heal in days; unrepaired ones take weeks.

title: Bunker Etiquette
body: Bunker etiquette preserves conditions for all players. Enter from low side nearest ball. After shot, rake all footprints and the area you disturbed. Rake toward bunker center, leaving sand smooth. Replace rake as course directs (inside or outside bunker). Leaving footprints for the next player is poor etiquette. Take time to rake properly.

title: Divot Repair and Etiquette
body: In fairway, repair or fill your divots. Replace the divot (put the turf piece back) or fill with sand/seed mix if provided. Divots in fairway: you must play ball as it lies—no free relief. Taking a divot is normal with irons; the key is repairing it. On practice ranges, follow the facility's divot pattern policy to maintain turf quality.

title: 14 Club Maximum
body: You may carry a maximum of 14 clubs. Penalty for excess: two strokes per hole played (max four strokes in stroke play); match play: deduction of holes. You can start with fewer than 14 and add during round if you don't delay play. You can replace a damaged club during round. Declare club 'out of play' if you find yourself over 14.

title: Playing Wrong Ball
body: Playing a wrong ball (not your ball) in stroke play: two-stroke penalty, then play correct ball. Strokes with wrong ball don't count. To avoid: mark your ball clearly, check brand and number before each shot. In match play: loss of hole. Exception: no penalty for wrong ball played from hazard if you correct before playing next shot.

title: Improving Lie or Stance
body: You cannot improve your lie, area of stance, or swing path by: moving, bending, or breaking anything growing or fixed, pressing down ground or sand, removing dew/frost/water. Exceptions: fairly taking stance (normal foot placement), making practice swing (touching grass is ok), pulling back branch if it returns when released. Penalties are two strokes or loss of hole.

title: Loose Impediments
body: Loose impediments (natural objects not fixed or growing: leaves, stones, twigs, insects) may be removed anywhere without penalty—including bunkers. You may move them by hand or with a club. If ball moves while removing impediment: in general area/green, replace without penalty. In bunker/penalty area, one-stroke penalty. Dew and snow are not loose impediments.

title: Movable Obstructions
body: Movable obstructions (artificial objects that can reasonably be moved: rakes, bottles, towels) may be removed. If ball moves during removal, replace without penalty. If ball lies in/on obstruction, lift ball, remove obstruction, drop ball where it was (or place on green). Free relief even in bunkers and penalty areas. No penalty for moving the obstruction.

title: Club Speed Explained
body: Club speed measures how fast the clubhead travels at impact, expressed in mph. Driver averages: PGA Tour ~115mph, amateur ~95mph. Higher club speed potential means more distance, but only if strike quality and launch conditions are good. To increase: improve sequencing, develop flexibility, train for speed. Club speed alone doesn't guarantee distance—strike quality matters more for most.

title: Ball Speed vs Club Speed
body: Ball speed is how fast the ball leaves the clubface at impact. It's the better predictor of distance than club speed because it captures both speed and strike quality. Ball speed = club speed × smash factor. If club speed is high but ball speed is low, focus on strike quality. If strike is solid but ball speed is low, work on speed or fitting.

title: Smash Factor Explained
body: Smash factor is ball speed divided by club speed—it measures energy transfer efficiency. Higher smash = more centered contact. Typical maxes: driver 1.50, irons 1.35-1.40. If your driver smash is 1.40, you're leaving distance on the table from off-center hits. Focus on strike quality before chasing speed. Smash factor is the easiest distance metric to improve.

title: Attack Angle (AoA)
body: Attack angle is the vertical direction of clubhead movement at impact. Positive = upward (hitting up), negative = downward (hitting down). Driver ideal: +2° to +5° upward for optimal launch/spin. Irons ideal: -2° to -5° downward for ball-first contact. Hitting down with driver adds spin and costs distance. Hitting up with irons causes thin shots.

title: Dynamic Loft at Impact
body: Dynamic loft is the actual loft presented to the ball at impact—not the club's static loft. It's affected by: shaft lean (forward lean = less dynamic loft), attack angle, face angle. More dynamic loft = higher launch, more spin. Less dynamic loft = lower launch, less spin. Better players typically deliver less dynamic loft (hands ahead at impact).

title: Launch Angle
body: Launch angle is the initial vertical angle the ball takes off relative to the ground. Affected by: loft, attack angle, strike location. Driver optimal: 12-15° typically. Higher launch with low spin maximizes carry. Too high with too much spin = balloon. Too low with too little spin = nose dive. Launch monitors help optimize your launch conditions.

title: Spin Rate Basics
body: Spin rate is how fast the ball rotates (rpm). Backspin creates lift (carries ball further) and stopping power. Driver optimal: 2000-2500 rpm for most speeds. Irons: 5000-8000+ rpm for stopping power. Too much driver spin = balloon, lost distance. Too little = ball doesn't carry or stop. Spin is influenced by: loft, attack angle, face contact, ball type.

title: Spin Loft: The Spin Generator
body: Spin loft is the angle between the clubface direction and the path of the club at impact. It's the primary creator of spin. Spin loft = dynamic loft minus attack angle. Higher spin loft = more spin. To reduce driver spin: hit up more (reduce spin loft) or use lower loft. Understanding spin loft explains why hitting down on driver adds spin.

title: Carry vs Total Distance
body: Carry distance is how far the ball flies in the air. Total distance adds rollout. Know both for each club. Course management uses carry (clearing hazards) and total (reaching targets). Wet conditions: more carry, less roll. Firm conditions: less carry needed, more roll. When club selection matters for hazards, use carry distance, not total.

title: Apex Height
body: Apex is the highest point of ball flight. Higher apex = steeper landing angle = more stopping power. Driver apex: 80-100 feet for most players. Wedges: 60-80 feet. Too low apex = running shots that don't hold greens. Too high = vulnerable to wind. Apex is determined by launch angle and spin—optimize both for controllable trajectories.

title: Descent and Landing Angle
body: Descent angle is the angle at which the ball approaches the ground. Steeper descent = more stopping power, less roll. Typical descent angles: driver 35-40°, 7-iron 45-50°, wedge 50-55°. Shallow descent (common with low spin driver) causes ball to run. Course management: firm greens need steeper descent to hold. Soft greens allow shallower approach.

title: Face to Path: Curve Generator
body: Face-to-path angle determines curve. If face is open to path = fade/slice (curves away from face). If face is closed to path = draw/hook (curves toward face). Amount of curve depends on difference between face and path. Example: path 5° right, face 2° right = face closed to path = draw. This is the fundamental ball flight law.

title: Club Path Explained
body: Club path is the horizontal direction the clubhead moves through impact relative to the target line. Positive path = in-to-out (right for righties). Negative path = out-to-in (left for righties). Path influences start direction (15-25%) and curve (through face-to-path relationship). Change path with: stance alignment, ball position, downswing sequence.

title: Face Angle Impact
body: Face angle at impact is where the clubface points relative to target line. Face determines 75-85% of starting direction. Open face = ball starts right of target (for righties). Closed face = ball starts left. Control face angle through: grip, wrist position, forearm rotation. Most players struggle with face control more than path—prioritize face work.

title: Dispersion and Standard Deviation
body: Dispersion describes your shot pattern—how widely shots scatter. Measured in standard deviation (SD): one SD contains 68% of shots, two SD contains 95%. If your 7-iron SD is 15 yards left-right, your total width is roughly 60 yards (2 SD each direction). Knowing your dispersion guides target selection—aim to keep 2 SD away from trouble.

title: Handicap Index Explained
body: Handicap Index measures your playing ability and allows fair competition. Calculated from best 8 of last 20 score differentials. Lower handicap = better player. Course Handicap adjusts your Index for course difficulty. Net score = gross score minus course handicap. Goal: your net score should be around par. Track your handicap to measure improvement over time.

title: Course Rating and Slope
body: Course Rating: expected score for a scratch golfer (0 handicap). Usually between 67-75. Slope Rating: difficulty for bogey golfer relative to scratch golfer. Range 55-155, standard is 113. Higher slope = harder for higher handicaps. Your Course Handicap = Index × (Slope/113). Ratings are set by golf associations using standardized methodology.

title: Greens in Regulation (GIR)
body: GIR means reaching the green in regulation: par minus 2 strokes. Par 3: 1 shot. Par 4: 2 shots. Par 5: 3 shots. Tour average: 65-70%. 20-handicap average: 25-30%. GIR is the strongest correlate with scoring. Track your GIR percentage to identify improvement areas. If you rarely hit GIR, focus on approach play, not putting or driving.

title: Fairways Hit Percentage
body: Fairway percentage tracks tee shot accuracy on par 4s and 5s. Tour average: 60-65%. Amateur average: 40-50%. Important because fairway lies give better approach shots. However, fairway percentage alone is misleading—driving distance also matters. Balance: 290 yards and 50% fairways may score better than 240 yards and 70% fairways. Track both metrics.

title: Strokes Gained Explained
body: Strokes Gained measures performance relative to a baseline (usually PGA Tour or scratch). Positive = better than baseline, negative = worse. Categories: Off-the-tee, Approach, Around-green, Putting. Shows where you're gaining or losing strokes. More useful than raw stats because it accounts for shot difficulty. Identify weakest area and prioritize practice there.

title: Up and Down Percentage
body: Up and down: getting the ball in the hole in two shots when you miss the green—typically a chip/pitch plus one putt. Tour average: 60%. Amateur average: 30-40%. This is the par-saving skill. Track your percentage and work on chipping and short putting. Improving from 30% to 45% saves multiple strokes per round.

title: Three-Putt Avoidance
body: Three-putts destroy scores. Tour average: 2-3% of greens. Amateur average: 10-15%. At 15%, you're losing 2-3 strokes per round to three-putts alone. Primary causes: poor lag putting (leaving long second putts) and poor green reading. Focus on getting first putt inside 3 feet. Track three-putt percentage—it's one of the easiest improvements to make.

title: Effective Range Practice
body: Quality over quantity. Start with wedges for tempo, work up to driver, finish with your first-tee club. Hit to targets, not into open space. Alternate shot types: high, low, draw, fade. Practice your actual shots, not just full swings. End each session with 10 'playing' shots: pick target, go through routine, hit one ball. Random practice transfers better than block practice.

title: Pre-Round Warmup
body: Arrive 30-45 minutes early. Dynamic stretching first: arm circles, hip rotations, torso twists. Range: start with wedge half-swings, build to full swings through the bag. 15-20 balls max—you're warming up, not practicing. End with first-tee club. Putting green: long lag putts for speed feel, then short putts for confidence. Walk to first tee loose and ready.

title: Lag Putting Drill
body: Distance control is the most important putting skill. Drill: place balls at 20, 30, 40 feet. Putt each trying to stop within 3-foot circle around hole (use tee markers). Focus on stroke length, not hitting at the ball. Feel the distance; don't calculate. Repeat until you consistently get within the circle. This skill eliminates three-putts.

title: Short Putt Confidence Drill
body: Short putts are about confidence and routine. Drill: place 4-5 balls in a circle, 3 feet from hole. Make all of them. If you miss, start over. Goal: make 20+ in a row. This builds trust. Variation: do this from different angles to see different breaks. Under pressure on course, recall this drill—you've made hundreds of these.

title: Gate Drill for Putting
body: Gate drill improves face control and start line. Place two tees just wider than putter head, 2-3 feet ahead of ball. Stroke putts through the gate. If you hit tees, your path or face is off. Successful strokes start ball on intended line. Progress: narrow the gate as you improve. This drill isolates start line from read—work on stroke first.

title: Chipping Landing Spot Drill
body: Chipping consistency comes from predictable landing spots. Place towel or club on green as target. Practice landing ball on the towel from various distances and lies. Use different clubs (7-iron through SW) to see how each rolls out. Build your mental library: 'From here, land it there, it rolls to the hole.' On course, pick landing spot before shot.

title: Wedge Distance Control Drill
body: Know your wedge distances at different swing lengths. Drill: hit 10 balls with PW at full swing—record average carry. Repeat at 3/4 swing, 1/2 swing. Do same for GW, SW. Build your wedge matrix. On course, pick the club and swing length that matches your distance need. Full committed swings at target beats tentative full swings.

title: Impact Position Drill
body: Good impact = shaft leaning forward, hands ahead of ball, weight on lead side. Drill: set up to ball, then move to impact position without swinging. Check: hands ahead, chest over ball, weight 80% on lead side. Hold this position. Now make slow swings through this impact checkpoint. This drill grooves proper feel for ball-first contact.

title: Alignment Stick Drills
body: Alignment sticks are the most versatile training aid. Uses: 1) Lay parallel to target line to check alignment. 2) Place along toe line to check stance. 3) Stick in ground on target line for path reference. 4) Hold against lead hip to feel proper turn. 5) Place outside ball to prevent over-the-top. Every range session should include alignment work.

title: Towel Under Arms Drill
body: Promotes connection between arms and body. Tuck small towel under both armpits. Make swings without dropping the towel. This prevents arms from separating from body rotation. If towel falls, your arms are overactive. Start with half swings, progress to full. Connected swings are more consistent because body controls arms rather than arms working independently.

title: Feet Together Drill
body: Feet together drill improves balance and tempo. Address ball with feet touching. Make smooth swings—poor balance will cause you to fall over. This drill eliminates sway, promotes rotation around spine, and forces good tempo. If you can make solid contact feet together, you have good fundamentals. Use as regular warmup or when struggling with contact.

title: One-Handed Drills
body: One-handed swings improve feel and coordination. Lead arm only: promotes body rotation, prevents chicken wing, builds strength. Trail arm only: promotes proper release, prevents casting, develops feel. Start with half swings, short clubs. Progress to fuller swings. These drills reveal which arm dominates incorrectly and train better coordination.

title: Slow Motion Swing Drill
body: Slow motion swings build awareness and muscle memory. Make full swings at 25% speed, feeling every position: takeaway, top, transition, impact, finish. Hold finish in balance. This reveals flaws hidden by speed and grooves proper positions. Use mirrors or video to check positions. Progress gradually: 25%, 50%, 75%, then full speed.

title: Pause at Top Drill
body: Pausing at the top of backswing improves transition timing. Make backswing, hold at top for 1-2 seconds, then swing through. This prevents rushing the transition, allows proper lower-body-first sequence, and builds awareness of top position. If you tend to snatch from the top or rush, this drill slows you down and improves timing.

title: Pump Drill for Lag
body: Pump drill trains downswing sequence and lag. Make backswing, start downswing to halfway point, pump back to top, then swing through. This grooves the feeling of lower body leading while hands stay back. Repeat pumps if needed. Prevents casting by training proper sequence. When struggling with fat shots or lack of power, use this drill.

title: Step Through Drill
body: Step through drill improves weight transfer. Take normal address. As you swing through, step toward target with trail foot, finishing with feet together and weight fully on lead side. This forces proper weight transfer and prevents hanging back. Exaggerated initially, but grooves the feeling of moving through the ball into a full finish.

title: Bunker Practice: Line in Sand
body: For greenside bunkers, draw a line in the sand where the ball would be. Practice splashing sand along the line without a ball. Goal: consistent entry point 1-2 inches behind the line, shallow divot through the line. Once pattern is consistent, add ball. The club should never touch the ball—the sand lifts it out. Confidence comes from consistent entry point.

title: 9-Shot Drill: Shape Control
body: Advanced drill for shot shaping. Hit 9 shots: low draw, mid draw, high draw, low straight, mid straight, high straight, low fade, mid fade, high fade. This develops feel for manipulating flight. Use on range with specific targets. Tour players can do this easily; it's a goal for serious amateurs. Start with just high/low, add draw/fade over time.

title: Scrambling Practice
body: Practice the shots you face on course: awkward lies, half-wedges, pressure putts. On practice green, drop balls in random locations and play to the hole—keep score. On range, practice different lies: uphill, downhill, tight. Create pressure: don't leave until you make 5 up-and-downs in a row. This transfers better than perfect-lie block practice.

title: Random vs Block Practice
body: Block practice: same shot repeatedly. Random practice: vary shot each time. Block feels productive but transfers poorly. Random practice feels harder but builds adaptable skills. On range: after warming up, play imaginary holes—tee shot, approach, chip, putt. Each shot is different. On course, you never hit the same shot twice consecutively. Train that way.

title: 15-Minute Practice Routine
body: Short on time? Focus on scoring zone. 5 minutes: lag putting to different distances, focusing on speed. 5 minutes: chipping from 3 positions around the green, different clubs. 5 minutes: short putts, making 15+ in a row from 3 feet. This 15-minute routine improves scoring more than an hour hitting drivers. Prioritize quality over quantity.

title: 30-Minute Practice Routine
body: Balanced 30-minute session. 5 minutes: wedges for tempo and contact. 8 minutes: mid-irons to specific targets, varying trajectories. 5 minutes: driver with focus on centerface contact. 7 minutes: putting—lag putts for distance, short putts for confidence. 5 minutes: chipping from various lies. Finish with the shot you'll use on first hole to build confidence.

title: 60-Minute Full Practice Session
body: Comprehensive practice session. 10 minutes: full warmup stretch and wedge warmup. 15 minutes: ball striking—work on a specific fault or build confidence. 10 minutes: driver with purpose (accuracy or distance work). 15 minutes: short game—bunker shots, chips from multiple positions, pitch shots. 10 minutes: putting—lag, short, breaking putts. End with strong finish.

title: Mental Rehearsal
body: Practice without a club: visualize shots. See the setup, feel the swing, watch the ball flight. Tour players do extensive mental rehearsal. Benefits: grooves neural patterns, builds confidence, allows practice anywhere. Before a round: visualize each hole, see yourself executing key shots. Before a difficult shot: rehearse mentally before physically. This is underutilized by amateurs.

title: Video Analysis for Self-Coaching
body: Video your swing for self-analysis. Down-the-line and face-on angles show different things. Compare to your favorite pro or your own best swings. Look for: alignment at address, position at top, path through impact, finish balance. Don't overanalyze—pick one thing to work on. Record progress over time. Slow motion reveals what your eyes can't see in real-time.

title: Practicing Your Weaknesses
body: Practice what you're bad at, not what you're good at. Identify your weakest area through stats: driving accuracy, approach proximity, up-and-down rate, three-putt rate. Dedicate 60%+ of practice to that weakness. Improvement comes from eliminating weak links. Hitting balls at the range feels good; grinding on weaknesses produces results. Be honest about where you need work.

title: Creating Practice Pressure
body: Pressure on course causes different performance than relaxed range practice. Create pressure in practice: compete with a friend, set consequences (start over if you miss), track stats and try to beat them. Example: don't leave putting green until you make 20 3-footers in a row. Practice should be harder than playing so playing feels easier.

title: Getting Feedback in Practice
body: Practice without feedback is just exercise. Get feedback through: impact tape/foot spray for strike location, video for positions, launch monitor for numbers, targets for accuracy. External feedback reveals what you can't feel. Don't trust feelings alone—they can be wrong. Use objective measures to confirm changes are working. Technology has made feedback accessible to everyone.

title: Setup Checkpoints for Consistency
