body: Before every swing, run through consistent setup checkpoints. 1) Clubface aimed at target. 2) Feet parallel left of target. 3) Ball position correct for club. 4) Weight balanced. 5) Knees slightly flexed. 6) Arms hanging naturally. 7) Chin up slightly. These should become automatic. Inconsistent setup leads to compensations mid-swing. Build a reliable foundation.

title: One-Piece Takeaway
body: The takeaway sets the tone for the entire swing. Move shoulders, arms, and club together as one unit for the first 12-18 inches. Club stays low to the ground, hands quiet. When hands reach hip height, club should point parallel to target line. Common fault: jerky hands-only takeaway. Feel like you're pushing the club away with your chest rotation.

title: Creating Width in Backswing
body: Width creates power and consistency. Keep lead arm relatively straight (not rigid) going back, reaching away from your body. At the top, hands should be high with extended arms, not collapsed against your body. Width creates arc length which increases clubhead speed. Drill: feel like you're reaching for the back wall during backswing.

title: The Transition: Key to Power
body: Transition from backswing to downswing is where power is generated. The lower body starts down while the club is still completing the backswing. This creates stretch in your core—storing energy. Feel: as hands reach the top, lead heel plants and hips start to rotate open. Rushing here loses power and causes over-the-top. Smooth transition is key.

title: Creating and Maintaining Lag
body: Lag is the angle between your trail forearm and the club shaft in the downswing. It stores energy for release at impact. Created by proper sequence—body leading, arms following. Maintained by letting hips rotate without casting hands. Lost by: hitting from the top, tension, trying to help ball up. Feel: hands leading clubhead into impact.

title: The Release Through Impact
body: The release is unhinging your wrists through impact, squaring the face and delivering speed. A proper release happens naturally when sequence and lag are correct. Avoid: manipulating hands to square face (timing dependent), holding off and blocking (loses speed). Feel: trail hand rotating over lead through impact, club flowing to finish. Trust the release.

title: Complete Your Follow Through
body: The follow-through reveals swing quality. Full follow-through with: weight on lead side, chest facing target, club behind head or over shoulder, balanced position held for 3+ seconds. Incomplete follow-through usually means deceleration or manipulation during swing. Practice finishing in balance every swing—make it a habit. The finish is a result of good swing, not an add-on.

title: Driver Setup Specifics
body: Driver setup differs from irons. Ball forward (off lead heel/instep), teed high (half ball above crown), wider stance for stability, spine tilted slightly away from target, weight slightly favoring trail side. This promotes ascending blow (hitting up on ball) which optimizes launch and reduces spin. Feel: hitting up and through, not down and on.

title: Sweeping Driver Swing
body: Driver swing is a sweeping motion, not a descending blow like irons. The ascending attack angle (hitting up) is created by ball position and spine tilt, not by trying to lift the ball. Swing through the ball toward target. Common mistake: trying to help ball up causes thin/topped shots. Trust the loft and setup; let the club do the work.

title: 3-Wood from Fairway
body: 3-wood from fairway requires clean contact. Setup: ball slightly back from driver position, weight centered, hands slightly ahead. The key: sweep the ball with a shallow angle, brushing grass where ball sits. Don't try to lift it—trust the loft. Consider: is a 5-wood or hybrid a safer choice from tight lies? 3-wood from rough is very difficult for most players.

title: 3-Wood off the Tee
body: 3-wood off the tee is a smart play on tight holes. Tee it low—just above grass level—for sweeping contact. The lower tee height promotes a shallower attack angle suited to 3-wood. Advantages over driver: higher loft is more forgiving, shorter shaft is easier to control. Sacrifice: 20-30 yards distance for accuracy. Use when fairway is the priority.

title: Hybrid from Various Lies
body: Hybrids shine from various lies where long irons struggle. From rough: the rounded sole glides through grass better than irons. From fairway: easier to launch than long irons. From tee: consistent option on short par 4s and par 3s. Setup: like a mid-iron with ball position center-forward. Swing: descending blow like an iron. Trust the club's forgiveness.

title: Iron Ball-First Contact
body: Pure iron shots contact ball first, then turf—creating a divot after the ball position. This descending blow compresses the ball for optimal launch and spin. Setup: hands slightly ahead of ball, weight favoring lead side. Feel: covering the ball with your chest through impact. Fat shots: low point too early. Thin shots: low point too late or standing up.

title: Pitching Wedge Versatility
body: The pitching wedge (44-48°) is your most versatile wedge. Uses: full approaches 120-140 yards, bump-and-run chips, long pitch shots, tight-lie greenside shots. Being comfortable with your PW in many situations builds confidence. Practice multiple trajectories and swing lengths. Most golfers should hit PW more than any other wedge—it's the workhorse.

title: Creating Wedge Spin
body: Spin comes from clean contact, proper equipment, and technique. Factors: fresh grooves, urethane-cover ball, descending angle of attack, speed through impact. High-handicappers often struggle to spin because of contact issues, not swing speed. Priority: ball-first contact with forward shaft lean. Clean the grooves frequently; replace wedges when grooves wear (typically 75+ rounds).

title: Putter Stroke Basics
body: A consistent putting stroke starts with setup: eyes over ball, arms hanging naturally, shoulders parallel to line. Stroke: pendulum motion from shoulders with quiet wrists. Back and through same length for distance control. Face should remain square to path throughout. Less movement means fewer variables. Keep lower body still and let shoulders rock.

title: Specialty Club Uses
body: Clubs can be used creatively beyond their design. Putter from off-green: Texas wedge when green is firm and flat to hole. Hybrid chip: bump-and-run with hybrid from tight lie. 3-wood punch: low running shot under branches. Open-face wedge: high soft shots. Learn to use clubs in multiple ways to handle unusual situations on the course.

title: Custom Fitting Benefits
body: Custom fitting optimizes clubs for your unique body and swing. Key measurements: height, wrist-to-floor, swing speed, ball flight tendency. Fitting session determines: shaft flex/weight, lie angle, length, grip size, head design. Custom fit clubs from a quality fitter often outperform premium off-the-rack sets. Worth the investment for any serious golfer.

title: Shaft Kick Point
body: Kick point (or flex point) is where the shaft bends most during the swing. High kick: lower ball flight, more control, preferred by faster swingers. Low kick: higher ball flight, easier to launch, helps slower swingers. Mid kick: balanced option. Match kick point to your desired trajectory and swing speed. Fitting helps determine your optimal kick point.

title: Club Maintenance Basics
body: Maintain clubs for best performance. Clean grooves after each round with brush and water—dirt reduces spin. Check grips for wear; replace when smooth or hard (typically annually for frequent players). Inspect shafts for damage. Store clubs properly, avoiding extreme temperatures. Well-maintained equipment performs better and lasts longer.

title: Putter Head Weight Effects
body: Heavier putter heads promote smoother strokes with less hand manipulation—good for fast greens and nervous putters. Lighter heads offer more feel and control—preferred on slower greens or by touch players. Counter-balanced (heavy grip end) helps reduce hand action. Many putters have adjustable weights. Experiment to find your preference.

title: Golf Ball Construction Types
body: Two-piece balls: distance-oriented, lower spin, more durable. Best for high handicappers who need straighter flight. Three-piece balls: balance of distance and spin. Good for mid-handicappers. Four/five-piece balls: maximum spin control around greens, softer feel. For skilled players who shape shots. Match ball to your skill level—tour balls don't help if you can't find the fairway.

title: Ball Compression Explained
body: Compression measures how much the ball deforms at impact. Low compression (70-80): softer feel, easier to compress for slower swing speeds. High compression (90-100+): firmer feel, better for faster swing speeds. Myth: you don't need to 'compress' high compression balls properly. Reality: any golfer can use any compression, but optimal match improves performance slightly.

title: Groove Design and Spin
body: Grooves channel away water and debris, creating friction for spin. Aggressive U-grooves provide more spin than V-grooves. Grooves wear over time, reducing spin—noticeable around 75+ rounds. Wedge grooves wear fastest due to sand and rough contact. Fresh grooves are essential for stopping power on approach shots. Consider new wedges annually if you play frequently.

title: Conservative vs Aggressive Strategy
body: Default to conservative strategy: aim for fat parts of fairways, center of greens. Switch to aggressive only when: your skill level supports it, the reward justifies risk, the penalty for miss is acceptable. Most amateurs are too aggressive. Calculate expected outcome, not best-case scenario. Conservative strategy produces lower average scores for typical players.

title: Playing Your Natural Shot Shape
body: Most golfers have a natural shot shape (fade or draw). Strategy: play that shape rather than fight it. If you fade, aim left side and let it work right. Trying to hit straight or against your tendency creates tension. Know your curve: if you fade 15 yards, aim 15 yards left. Working with your tendency is easier than changing it.

title: Trouble Recovery Strategy
body: When in trouble, priority is back in play. Don't compound errors with heroic attempts. Evaluate: what's the highest-percentage shot to fairway or green? Often that's a punch sideways, not a miracle through trees. Accept the stroke penalty of the mistake rather than risking more. The difference between bogey and double bogey is huge over 18 holes.

title: Late Round Strategy
body: Closing holes determine your score. If you need pars to shoot your target, play smart: club down off tees for fairways, aim at center greens, lag putt to avoid three-putts. If you need birdies, become slightly more aggressive but not reckless. Don't let emotions make decisions. Stick to process; the outcome will follow.

title: First Hole Strategy
body: First hole jitters affect everyone. Strategy: prioritize a smooth start over heroics. Hit your most reliable tee club even if it's not driver. Accept that first hole is about getting into the round, not winning it. Make a smooth swing focused on tempo. Bogey on first hole isn't a disaster; a blow-up number is. Play within yourself until you're warmed up.

title: Identifying Scoring Holes
body: Scoring holes are your birdie opportunities: short par 4s, reachable par 5s, short par 3s. Study the course—know which holes suit your game. Strategy: play these holes with slightly more aggression, take calculated risks. On difficult holes, make par your goal. Gaining strokes on scoring holes while protecting on hard holes is the winning formula.

title: Match Play Strategy Differences
body: Match play strategy differs from stroke play. You play the opponent, not the course. If opponent is in trouble, play safe—let them make mistakes. If you're behind, take more risk. If they have a birdie putt, be aggressive for your birdie. Don't concede anything psychologically. Play one hole at a time; deficits can be erased. Strategic aggression based on opponent's situation.

title: Playing in Cold vs Hot Weather
body: Temperature affects ball flight. Cold air: denser, ball flies shorter (lose ~2 yards per 10°F drop). Ball is also firmer and harder to compress. Take extra club. Hot air: thinner, ball flies farther. Factor temperature into club selection. Also consider your body: cold muscles are tight—swing smoother, don't force. Stay warm between shots.

title: Playing at Altitude
body: Higher altitude means thinner air—ball flies farther and higher. General rule: 2% more distance per 1,000 feet of elevation. At 5,000 feet, add 10% to your distances. Spin effect is less, so ball may not stop as quickly. Mountain courses also often have elevation changes within holes—add those calculations too. Ask locals for guidance on first visit.

title: Playing from Tight Lies
body: Tight lies (hardpan, bare dirt, thin grass) demand precision. The margin for error is reduced—fat shots are disasters. Strategy: play ball slightly back, use less lofted club than normal for same distance, make crisp descending contact. Avoid: lob wedge shots (too much bounce), trying to help ball up. Punch-style shots with mid-irons are safer.

title: Escaping Deep Rough
body: Deep rough wraps around clubhead, closing face and grabbing shaft. Strategy: take a lofted club and advance it to the fairway—don't be a hero. Setup: ball back, open clubface to counteract grass closing it. Steep descending blow to cut through grass. Expect shorter distance. If ball is buried, your only goal is getting back to fairway.

title: Recognizing Flyer Lies
body: Flyer lie: ball sitting up in light rough with grass behind it. Grass gets between clubface and ball, reducing spin. Result: ball launches higher and releases more—can fly 10-20 yards farther than expected. Recognition: can you see grass behind the ball? Strategy: take less club, aim for front of green, expect more roll.

title: Stroke and Distance Penalty Explained
body: Stroke and distance: add one penalty stroke AND replay from the original position. Used for: out of bounds, lost ball. Example: tee shot goes OB—you're hitting 3 from the tee. This is the harshest penalty in golf. Strategy: avoid OB like the plague; it's worse than a penalty area where relief options exist. When OB is tight, club down for control.

title: Red vs Yellow Penalty Areas
body: Yellow stakes: two relief options with one stroke penalty—back-on-line or stroke-and-distance. Red stakes: add lateral relief option—drop within two club-lengths of crossing point, not nearer hole. Red areas typically parallel fairway; yellow areas cross fairway (like water in front of green). Know the difference; red gives you more options.

title: Free Relief Situations
body: Free relief (no penalty) is available from: immovable obstructions (cart paths, sprinkler heads), abnormal course conditions (temporary water, GUR), embedded ball in general area. Procedure: find nearest point of complete relief, drop within one club-length, not nearer hole. Know your rights—free relief can turn a disaster into a manageable shot.

title: Sprinkler Head Relief
body: Sprinkler heads are immovable obstructions. If they interfere with your stance, swing, or ball lies on them, you get free relief. Find nearest point where no interference exists, drop within one club-length. If sprinkler is just in your line of play (not stance/swing), no relief except on putting green where you can place the ball.

title: When Ball Moves
body: If your ball moves: on putting green—replace without penalty. In general area by natural forces (wind)—play from new position. If you caused it while searching—replace with one-stroke penalty. At address if you caused movement—one-stroke penalty, replace ball. Key: if you caused it, penalty; if nature caused it on green, replace; elsewhere, play it.

title: Practice Swing Accidents
body: If your practice swing accidentally moves your ball: in the general area—one-stroke penalty, replace ball. On the putting green—no penalty, replace ball. Best practice: don't take practice swings too close to your ball. If you accidentally move your ball, don't compound the error—know the rule and replace it properly.

title: Playing from Penalty Areas
body: You can always play your ball from a penalty area without penalty. Before stroke: you may touch loose impediments, may ground club or touch water with club. You may not: test the condition intentionally. After stroke: if ball stays in penalty area, you can play it again or take relief. Taking relief adds one penalty stroke.

title: Animal Damage Relief
body: Animal damage (holes, tracks, mounds from animals) in the general area may give free relief if it interferes with lie, stance, or swing. Find nearest point of relief, drop within one club-length. On putting green, you may also repair animal damage. Note: this applies to damage, not the animal itself blocking your shot.

title: Advice Rules
body: During a round, you may not give or ask for advice from anyone except your caddie or partner. Advice is anything that might influence decisions about play, club selection, or shot method. You may ask anyone about rules, distances, or location of hazards (public information). Penalty for advice: two strokes in stroke play, loss of hole in match play.

title: Pace of Play Guidelines
body: Expected pace: 4 hours for 18 holes (cart), 4:15 walking. Tips: keep up with group ahead (not just ahead of group behind). Be ready when it's your turn—pre-plan shot while others play. Walk briskly between shots. Limit practice swings to one or two. Continuous putting when appropriate. Search limit is 3 minutes. Don't delay others.

title: Music and Phones on Course
body: Personal music is allowed but must not distract others or slow play. Use one earbud; keep volume low. Phone use for scoring/distance apps is fine. Phone calls should be brief and away from other players. Talking loudly on phones while others play is poor etiquette. When in doubt, prioritize respect for playing partners and pace.

title: Posting Scores for Handicap
body: Post all scores from rounds of at least 9 holes played under the Rules of Golf. Include penalty scores (not returned due to weather, for example). Don't cherry-pick only good rounds—the system uses best differentials. Playing alone? You can still post scores. Accurate posting creates a fair handicap that represents your ability.

title: Shot Pattern Analysis
body: Your shot pattern shows tendencies. Track: how many shots go left/right of target, how far offline, typical miss direction. Most golfers have consistent miss patterns. Once you know your pattern, play for it—aim to put your center shot on target knowing your pattern will scatter around it. Pattern awareness improves course management.

title: Sweet Spot and Center Face
body: The sweet spot is the point on the clubface that produces maximum energy transfer. For most clubs, it's slightly above geometric center. Hitting the sweet spot: maximum ball speed, lowest twist, straightest flight. Modern clubs enlarge the sweet spot through MOI (moment of inertia) design. Use impact tape to check your typical strike location.

title: Understanding Sidespin
body: Sidespin causes curve. Left spin (for righties): ball curves left (draw/hook). Right spin: ball curves right (fade/slice). Spin axis tilt creates sidespin—not the ball literally spinning sideways. Caused by face-to-path difference. 0 axis tilt = no curve. More tilt = more curve. Control curve by controlling face relative to path.

title: Moment of Inertia (MOI)
body: MOI measures a clubhead's resistance to twisting on off-center hits. Higher MOI: less twist, more forgiveness, straighter shots on mishits. Achieved by: larger heads, perimeter weighting. Lower MOI: more workability, more feel, less forgiving. Game improvement clubs maximize MOI; tour players sometimes prefer lower MOI for shot shaping control.

title: Center of Gravity (CG)
body: CG is the balance point of the clubhead. Low CG: higher launch, more spin (good for drivers needing launch help). High CG: lower launch, less spin. Forward CG: lower spin. Back CG: higher spin, more forgiveness. Adjustable weight drivers let you move CG. Understanding CG helps explain why certain clubs produce different ball flights.

title: Effective Loft at Impact
body: Effective loft (dynamic loft) is actual loft at impact—affected by shaft lean and attack angle. More shaft lean forward = less effective loft. More shaft lean back = more effective loft. Better players deliver less effective loft (hands ahead) creating compressed, lower-spinning shots. High handicappers often add loft at impact (scooping).

title: Toe Droop Effect
body: During the swing, centrifugal force causes the shaft to droop downward, especially at the toe. This changes lie angle at impact vs address—the toe drops, making effective lie more upright. Club fitters account for this when measuring lie angle dynamically rather than statically. Dynamic fitting is more accurate than static measurements alone.

title: Distance Control Practice
body: Distance control wins scoring battles. Drill: pick three targets at different distances. Hit to each in sequence without looking at targets between shots—rely on feel. Track how close you get. Progress: create distance ladder—hit PW 50, 75, 100 yards, etc. Develop feel for fractional swings. This is more valuable than hitting balls for distance.

title: Always Practice to Targets
body: Never hit balls without a target. Range balls into open space teaches nothing—you don't get feedback. Pick specific targets for every shot: flags, markers, yardage signs. Make the target smaller than you need—'aim small, miss small.' Evaluate each shot relative to target. This develops precision mindset that transfers to course.

title: Bunker Distance Control
body: Bunker distance control comes from swing length and sand amount. Short shots: small swing, enter closer to ball. Long shots: bigger swing, enter further behind ball. Practice: drop balls at 10, 20, 30 feet from flag. Hit to each distance. Feel the difference in swing size and entry point. This builds the touch needed for varied bunker shots.

title: Green Reading Practice
body: Green reading improves with practice. On practice green: before putting, commit to a read and call your break amount out loud. See if ball breaks that much. Recalibrate your reads based on results. Also practice from all angles around holes to see multiple break types. Most amateurs under-read break—consciously play more break initially.

title: Up and Down Challenge
body: Practice pressure up-and-downs. Drop 5 balls in different positions around practice green. Try to get up and down from all 5 (chip plus one putt). If you succeed, move to harder positions. Keep stats over sessions. This replicates real course pressure better than block practice. Goal: consistently get 3 of 5 up and down.

title: Pre-Round Putting Warmup
body: Pre-round putting warmup establishes feel for the day. Start with lag putts: roll balls to fringe and back, feeling speed. Then mid-range: 15-25 footers, note break and speed. Finally short putts: make 10 in a row from 3 feet for confidence. Don't work on mechanics—warm up and read the greens. Take notes on speed (faster/slower than usual).

title: Tee Drill for Contact
body: For iron contact, place a tee in ground 4 inches ahead of ball. Goal: strike ball, then brush/knock over the tee. This ensures low point is forward of ball for proper compression. If you can't reach the tee, low point is too early (fat tendency). Practice until you consistently contact ball then tee.

title: Mirror Work for Positions
body: Use a mirror for position work without hitting balls. Check: setup (posture, alignment), takeaway position, top of backswing, impact position, finish. Compare to photos of proper positions or your best swings. Mirror work builds awareness and allows slow, deliberate position training. Follow with actual swings on range to ingrain feels.

title: Practicing Bad Lies
body: Real golf includes bad lies—practice them. On range: create divot holes to practice from. At facility: practice from rough at various depths, uphill/downhill lies if available. Vary your typical practice position. When you face a bad lie on course, you'll have experience. Perfect-lie-only practice leaves you unprepared for reality.

title: Scoring Zone Priority
body: Most scoring improvement comes from inside 100 yards. Allocate practice time accordingly: 50% short game and putting, 30% wedges and short irons, 20% long clubs. This is opposite of typical amateur practice. The shots you hit most should get most practice. Track your practice time allocation and adjust toward scoring zone.

title: Adapting to Course Conditions
body: Every course plays different. Assess at start: green speed (fast/slow), firmness (hard/soft), rough depth, wind patterns. Adjust strategy accordingly. Fast greens: more conservative putting pace. Soft greens: attack pins. Deep rough: club down for escape. Course setup changes daily—what worked last time may not work today. Observe and adapt.

title: Playing in Wet Conditions
body: Wet conditions change everything. Ball: flies shorter from wet clubface, less roll on landing. Greens: slower, hold shots better but can plug. Stance: secure footing before swinging. Strategy: take extra club, aim at pins more aggressively (balls stop), play for less roll on chips. Keep grips and hands dry. Adjust expectations—wet rounds score higher.

title: Playing Firm and Fast Courses
body: Firm, fast courses require different strategy. Ball runs more on fairways—control over distance. Greens don't hold as well—land shots short and let them release to pins. Bump-and-run is more effective than high lofted shots. Putting pace is crucial on fast greens. Club selection: think about where ball will end up after roll, not just carry.

title: Par 3 Strategy
body: Par 3s test accuracy more than distance. Strategy: identify bail-out area (safe miss), aim there unless you're confident. Club selection priority: be enough club to reach middle of green—short is usually worse than long. Factor wind heavily; par 3s often have exposed greens. Don't be afraid to aim at center, not flag, for consistent pars.

title: Par 4 Strategy Framework
body: Par 4 strategy depends on hole length and layout. Short par 4 (<350 yards): accuracy off tee, wedge approach—be aggressive. Medium par 4 (350-420): balance of distance and position, mid-iron approach. Long par 4 (>420): fairway is essential, make par your goal. Always identify danger and plan to avoid it while leaving manageable approach.

title: Bunker Avoidance Strategy
body: Strategy should account for bunkers. Fairway bunkers: lose distance but playable—calculate risk of bringing them into play. Greenside bunkers: short-sided greenside bunker is disaster—aim to leave ball on opposite side if you miss. Deep bunkers, buried lies, high lips: avoid at all costs. Know which bunkers are penalties vs inconveniences.

title: Water Hazard Strategy
body: Water requires honest self-assessment. Can I carry it with my typical shot, not my best shot? If no, lay up. If yes, how much margin? Aim to clear by at least 10 yards. Consider: what happens if I'm slightly long? Sometimes water guards front but there's room behind. Plan approach based on both hazard location and recovery options.

title: Eye Dominance in Golf
body: Your dominant eye affects alignment perception. To test: point at distant object with both eyes open, close each eye—dominant eye keeps finger on target. If right-eye dominant with right-handed stance, you see the line accurately. If cross-dominant, you may misalign. Awareness helps: some players adjust head position to favor dominant eye's view of target line.

title: The Nine Ball Flights
body: Every shot is one of nine flights: push, push-draw, push-fade, straight, draw, fade, pull, pull-draw, pull-fade. Path determines start direction tendency; face-to-path determines curve. Understanding which flight you hit tells you what to fix. Straight is actually hardest—most players should optimize their natural curve rather than chase straight.

title: Quiet Hands Through Impact
body: Quiet hands means minimal manipulation through impact. Body rotation squares the face; hands are passive. Over-active hands cause inconsistency—timing dependent. Feel: hands transport the club while body controls face angle. Drill: half swings with focus on keeping wrist angles constant through impact. Let rotation do the work.

title: Staying Down Through the Shot
body: Staying down means maintaining spine angle through impact. Coming out of posture causes thin/topped shots. Feel: chest covers ball through impact, head stays relatively still until well after contact. It doesn't mean keeping head locked down rigidly—that restricts rotation. Feel: staying in your posture while rotating through.

title: Accelerating Through Impact
body: The club should be accelerating through impact, not decelerating. Deceleration causes: inconsistent contact, less spin, weak shots. Causes of decel: doubt, trying to steer, fear of outcome. Fix: commit to shot, make a full finish, trust your swing. If you're tentative, you've already lost. Full commitment beats perfect mechanics executed timidly.

title: Acceptable Head Movement
body: Some head movement is normal and even necessary. Slight movement away from target in backswing, then through toward target in downswing. What to avoid: excessive lateral sway, lifting up, dramatic drops. The head moves with your pivot—keep it relatively centered but don't lock it rigidly. Tension from trying to freeze head hurts more than slight movement.

title: Club Delivery Path
body: How the club is delivered to impact determines ball flight. Key checkpoints: halfway down, shaft should be parallel to target line and below hands. At impact: shaft lean forward with irons, hands ahead of ball, hips open, chest rotating through. Poor delivery: over the top (shaft outside hands), stuck inside (path too in-to-out).

title: Fairway Finder Strategy
body: A fairway finder is your reliable tee club when driver is risky. Usually 3-wood, hybrid, or long iron. Requirements: you hit it solidly 80%+ of the time, it stays in play. Practice this club enough to trust it under pressure. Having a go-to club for tight holes eliminates stress and prevents blow-up holes from errant drivers.

title: Utility Iron Uses
body: Utility irons (driving irons, 2-irons) offer low, penetrating flight with more control than hybrids. Uses: tee shots on windy days, low punch shots, running approaches. Setup: ball slightly back, hands ahead. Require solid contact—not forgiving. Good for better players who want a penetrating option; most amateurs prefer hybrid forgiveness.

title: Varying Chip Clubs
body: Don't always chip with the same club. Club selection based on ratio of carry to roll needed. 7-iron: lots of roll, little air time. PW: balanced carry and roll. SW: more air, less roll. Calculate: how far to landing spot vs how far to roll. Match club to the math. One-club chipping limits your options around greens.

title: Texas Wedge: Putting Off the Green
body: Texas wedge means using putter from off the green. When to use: flat or slightly uphill path, short grass between ball and green, firm conditions, no obstacles. Advantages: most consistent contact, predictable roll. Execute like a long putt—firm enough to get through fringe. Conservative but effective when conditions allow.

title: Trouble Club Selection
body: When in trouble, select the club that maximizes probability of advancing significantly while minimizing further trouble. Usually a mid-iron: enough loft to escape, controllable trajectory. Avoid: driver/woods from trouble (too hard to control), lob wedge (high risk of mishit). Accept the penalty stroke of your mistake; don't compound it.

title: Adjustable Driver Settings
body: Modern drivers offer adjustable: loft (±2°), lie angle, face angle, weight positioning. Use these to optimize your ball flight. Fighting slice? Close face, move weight to heel. Need more launch? Add loft, move weight back. Changes are small but meaningful. Experiment on range, not course. Once dialed in, leave settings alone.

title: Shaft Torque Explained
body: Torque measures shaft's resistance to twisting (in degrees). High torque: more twist, softer feel, can help square face for slicers. Low torque: less twist, firmer feel, more control for faster swingers. Driver shafts: 3-5° typical. Iron shafts: lower torque generally. Match torque to your swing speed and desired feel.

title: Driver Face Technology
body: Modern driver faces flex for more ball speed. Variable thickness faces: thin center for speed, thick edges for stability. AI-designed faces optimize flex patterns. Spring effect (COR) is limited by rules to 0.830. Face material: titanium for strength and flex. Technology helps mishits perform better, but center hits still reign supreme.

title: Wedge Setup Recommendations
body: Typical wedge setup for most players: PW (45-47°), GW (50-52°), SW (54-56°), LW (58-60°). Gap between wedges: 4-6 degrees for consistent yardage gaps. Consider bounce: high bounce for soft conditions/steep swingers, low bounce for firm conditions/shallow swingers. Three wedges minimum; four is standard for serious players.

title: Putter Head Styles
body: Blade putters: classic design, compact head, suits arc stroke, more feel, less forgiveness. Mallet putters: larger head, higher MOI, suits straight stroke, more forgiveness. Mid-mallet: balanced option. Face-insert vs milled: insert for softer feel, milled for firmer feedback. Choose style that matches your stroke and builds confidence.

title: Ball Selection by Conditions
body: Wind: lower spinning ball reduces ballooning. Wet: softer cover for grip on wet wedge shots. Firm greens: higher spin for stopping power. Fast greens: softer ball for better feel on touch shots. Cold weather: lower compression compresses easier. Consider conditions when selecting ball model, though consistency matters more for most amateurs.

title: Into Wind Club Selection
body: Into strong wind, club up significantly and swing easier. Hard swings add spin; spin balloons in wind. Example: 150-yard shot into 20mph wind might need 170-180 club hit at 80% effort. Ball flight: lower, more controlled. Also consider: knockdown shot with extra club for even more control. Don't fight the wind—use it strategically.

title: Crosswind Strategy
body: Two approaches to crosswind. 1) Aim into wind, let it bring ball back—simplest, reliable. 2) Curve ball into wind for straighter flight—requires shot shaping skill. Consider: which side has trouble? If trouble is downwind side, be extra careful. For high shots (wedges), wind effect is greater—compensate more.

title: Dogleg Strategy
body: Doglegs require strategic tee shots. Cut the corner? Calculate: can I carry the corner with margin? What's in the corner (trees, bunkers, OB)? What approach does cutting leave vs playing safe? Often, playing to the corner angle with controlled club leaves ideal approach angle. Cutting corners is high risk/reward—know your tendencies.

title: Short Par 4 Strategy
body: Short par 4s offer birdie opportunities but also danger if aggressive. Options: 1) Driver for eagle/birdie chance, risking trouble near green. 2) Iron/hybrid to ideal wedge distance for controlled birdie try. Consider: how well are you driving today? What trouble guards the green? Controlled aggression often beats max aggression.

title: Long Par 4 Approach
body: Long par 4s (440+ yards) are scoring challenges. Strategy: fairway is essential—mid-iron approach from rough is very difficult. Make par your goal; birdie is bonus. If you can't reach green in regulation, lay up to comfortable wedge distance rather than forcing long iron. Accept the hole's difficulty; don't compound with big numbers.

title: Finishing Hole Strategy
body: 18th hole carries psychological weight. Strategy varies by situation. Protecting good round: conservative play, avoid disasters. Chasing score: calculate whether aggressive play helps enough. Match play: consider opponent's situation. Don't change your process—stick to routine. One more hole deserves same focus as first 17.

title: Links Course Strategy
body: Links courses play different: firm/fast, windy, minimal trees, deep bunkers. Strategy: embrace ground game (bump and run), plan for wind on every shot, avoid pot bunkers absolutely, use slopes to funnel balls. Club selection: knockdown shots are valuable. Links rewards creativity and shot-making over pure power.

title: Desert Course Strategy
body: Desert courses feature: firm conditions, limited rough, severe penalties for missing fairway (rocks, cacti, unplayable lies). Strategy: accuracy over distance off tee, target line avoids desert areas entirely. From desert: often best to chip out sideways rather than attempt hero shot. Stroke and distance beats multiple penalty strokes.

title: Playing Around Trees
body: Trees in your line require decision: go over, under, around? Consider: height needed, gap size, risk of worse lie if you hit tree. Often safest play: low punch to fairway, accept the half-stroke loss. If attempting to go over/through: commit fully—half-hearted attempts hit trees. Have a clear picture of required shot before swinging.

title: Nearest Point of Complete Relief
body: Nearest point of complete relief is reference point for free relief. It's the closest point where: stance, swing, and lie are clear of the condition, no nearer the hole. You must use nearest point even if result is unfavorable (like rough). Determine by using the club you would have used for the shot. Mark it, then measure club-length from there.

title: Club-Length Measurement
body: Relief areas use club-lengths. Measure with longest club in your bag except putter (usually driver). Don't use putter even if it's technically longest. One club-length for most relief; two club-lengths for penalty area lateral relief and unplayable options. The club-length determines your relief area—ball must stay within it after drop.

title: Searching for Your Ball
body: You have 3 minutes to search for your ball. Time starts when you reach the area and begin searching. If ball not found in 3 minutes, it's lost—return to previous spot (stroke and distance). You may move loose impediments and some things during search. If you accidentally move ball while searching: no penalty, replace ball.

title: Identifying Your Ball
body: You must be able to identify your ball. If you can't tell if it's yours, you may mark and lift it to identify. Announce your intention, let opponent/marker observe, mark the spot, lift only enough to identify. If it's yours, replace it. If not yours, ball is lost. Clean only enough to identify—not more.

title: Playing from Wrong Green
body: If your ball is on a wrong putting green (a green other than the hole you're playing), you must take free relief. Find nearest point off the green, no nearer hole, and drop within one club-length. You cannot play from a wrong green—it protects the surface. No penalty for this mandatory relief.

title: Double Hit Rule
body: If you accidentally hit the ball twice in one stroke (double hit), there's no penalty—count only one stroke. The ball plays as it lies. This is a relatively recent rule change (2019). Previously, each contact counted as a stroke. Now, accidental multiple contacts are treated as one stroke regardless of number of times you contacted the ball.

title: Caddie Responsibilities and Rules
body: Your caddie may: give advice, carry equipment, search for ball, repair pitch marks, remove loose impediments. Caddie may not: touch ground in bunker when ball is there, stand behind you while making stroke, position on extension of line of play while you prepare. You're responsible for caddie's actions. Penalties apply to you.

title: Ball Striking Flagstick
body: As of 2019, you may leave the flagstick in when putting from anywhere—including on the green. If ball hits the flagstick, there's no penalty. Some studies suggest leaving it in helps more than hurts for most putts. You decide: leave in, have someone attend, or have it removed. Personal preference, but it's no longer mandatory to remove.

title: Relief Options Summary
body: Relief categories: Free relief—cart path, GUR, temporary water, embedded ball. Penalty relief (1 stroke)—penalty areas, unplayable lie. Stroke and distance—OB, lost ball. Know which relief applies to your situation. When in doubt, play provisional for potential lost ball/OB. Relief options save strokes when you know them.

title: Scoring Average
body: Scoring average is your mean score across rounds. More useful than single round scores for assessing ability. Tour average: around 70. Scratch average: 72-74. 10 handicap average: ~82. Track your scoring average over time to see improvement. Requires consistent conditions to be meaningful—adjust for course difficulty if tracking across multiple courses.

title: Proximity to Hole
body: Proximity measures average distance from hole after approach shots. PGA Tour average: ~30 feet from 150 yards. Amateur average: ~50+ feet. Lower proximity = more birdie putts. Track your proximity by club: where do your 7-irons end up vs wedges? This identifies which distances need work. Proximity is key to scoring improvement.

title: Scrambling Percentage
body: Scrambling is making par or better after missing the green in regulation. PGA Tour average: ~60%. Scratch amateur: ~40-45%. High handicap: ~25-30%. Scrambling encompasses chipping, pitching, bunker play, and short putting—your entire short game. Improving from 30% to 40% scrambling can save 2-3 strokes per round.

title: Putts Per Round
body: Average putts per round varies by handicap. Tour: ~28-29 putts. Scratch: ~31-32. 15 handicap: ~33-35. 25 handicap: ~36+. But context matters: hitting more greens means more putts but also more birdie chances. More meaningful: putts per GIR (how many putts after hitting green). Track for true putting assessment.

title: Driving Distance Stats
body: Average driving distance: PGA Tour ~295 yards, amateur ~215 yards. Distance matters but accuracy matters more for scoring. The sweet spot: enough distance to have reasonable approach clubs, enough accuracy to hit fairways. For most amateurs, improving accuracy beats chasing distance. Know your average, not your longest—plan from average.

title: Sand Save Percentage
body: Sand save is making par or better from greenside bunkers. PGA Tour average: ~50%. Amateur average: ~15-25%. Low sand save indicates either bunker technique problems or leaving in bad positions. Practice: consistent splash technique and distance control. Improving bunker play removes fear and saves strokes.

title: Approach Shot Statistics
body: Approach shots are the biggest scoring determinant. Track: GIR percentage, proximity to hole by distance (100-125, 125-150, etc.), miss pattern (short/long/left/right). Most amateurs miss short and right. Identifying patterns directs practice. Approach stats predict scoring better than driving stats for most skill levels.

title: Bounce Angle Details
body: Bounce angle is measured from leading edge to sole's lowest point. Degrees vary: 4-8° (low), 8-12° (mid), 12-16° (high). More bounce lifts leading edge, preventing digging. Less bounce allows leading edge to contact ball first on tight lies. Match to conditions and swing: diggers and soft conditions = high bounce; pickers and firm lies = low bounce.

title: Basic Bunker Technique
body: Greenside bunker fundamentals: open stance 20-30°, open clubface, ball forward, aim 1-2 inches behind ball. Swing along your body line (left for righties), letting club splash through sand under the ball. The club never touches the ball—sand lifts it out. Follow through fully; don't quit on the shot. Practice consistent entry point.

title: Bunker Distance Control
body: Bunker distance varies by: swing length, sand depth taken, clubface openness. Short shots: small swing, enter closer to ball. Long shots: bigger swing, enter further behind, less open face. Practice hitting to targets at 10, 20, 30 feet. Feel the difference. Consistent technique with varied swing length = distance control.

title: Basic Pitch Shot Technique
body: Pitch shot: ball forward of center, slight shaft lean, weight slightly forward. Swing: hinge wrists going back, unhinge through impact, accelerate through the ball. Contact: ball first, then turf (shallow divot after ball). Finish: hands and club head high. Don't scoop; trust the loft. The bounce should skip through turf, not dig.

title: Flop Shot Technique
body: Flop shot: high, soft landing with minimal roll. Setup: open stance significantly, open face fully, ball forward. Swing: along body line, accelerating through with high finish. Contact: slide bounce under ball on shallow angle. Warning: high risk—requires perfect execution. Only use when absolutely necessary. Practice extensively before deploying on course.

title: Basic Chip Technique
body: Chip shot: ball back of center, hands ahead, weight forward, narrow stance. Minimal wrist action—rock shoulders like a putt. Strike: descending blow, ball then turf. Ball comes out low, runs to the hole. Club selection determines roll: less loft = more roll. Keep it simple; consistent contact is the priority.

title: Speed Training Basics
body: To increase swing speed, train specifically for speed. Overspeed training: swing lighter club or alignment stick as fast as possible. Heavy training: swing weighted club to build strength. Contrast training: alternate heavy and light. Sessions: 2-3x per week, don't combine with regular practice. Speed gains take weeks—be consistent. Gains of 3-7 mph are realistic.

title: Golf Flexibility Routine
body: Golf-specific flexibility targets: hips (rotation), thoracic spine (rotation), shoulders (range of motion), hamstrings (forward bend). Daily routine: 10 minutes of hip circles, seated twists, shoulder stretches, hamstring stretches. Hold each 30 seconds. Improved flexibility = fuller turn, more power, fewer compensations. Most amateurs are too tight to make efficient swings.

title: Tracking Your Statistics
body: Track stats to identify weaknesses. Essential stats: fairways hit, GIR, putts per round, up-and-down percentage. Advanced: proximity by distance, scrambling by lie type, three-putt rate. Apps make tracking easy. Review weekly: where are you losing strokes? Allocate practice time to weakest area. Data-driven improvement beats random practice.

title: Practice Round Strategies
body: Practice rounds should simulate competition conditions. Play one ball, follow all rules. But also: experiment with club selections, play different lines, note yardages, test different approaches to each hole. Take notes on course strategy. The goal is learning the course while also testing your game under realistic conditions.

title: Building a Putting Routine
body: Consistent putting routine reduces variables. Example: read the putt from behind, pick your line and speed, take two practice strokes feeling the distance, address ball, one look at hole, stroke. Same routine every putt. Time: under 20 seconds. Routines reduce nerves and build confidence through familiarity.

title: Wedge Clock System
body: Clock system for wedge distances: 7:30 = quarter swing, 9:00 = half swing, 10:30 = three-quarter swing. Build your matrix: each wedge × each swing length = specific yardage. Example: SW at 9:00 = 65 yards, at 10:30 = 80 yards. Practice until distances are automatic. This replaces feel with system.

title: Consistent Pre-Shot Routine
body: Pre-shot routine should be identical every shot. Elements: stand behind ball (read shot), approach from side, set clubface first then feet, one or two looks at target, swing. Time it: 15-25 seconds ideal. Same routine for driver and wedge. Under pressure, routine provides structure. Deviation from routine signals doubt—step away and restart.

title: Improvement Between Rounds
body: Between rounds, focus on one thing. If you struggled with: driving—10 minutes of alignment work. Irons—work on ball-first contact with tee drill. Short game—20 chips and 20 lag putts. Don't overhaul everything. Identify the biggest leak and plug it. Small targeted improvements compound over time.

title: Rain Strategy Adjustments
body: Rain changes strategy: greens are slower (putt more aggressively), ball doesn't run (take more club), rough grabs more (take penalty and advance), grips get slippery (keep them dry). Mental: accept higher scores, don't force shots, patience is key. Play for the conditions everyone faces, not the score you wanted.

title: Hot Weather Strategy
body: Heat affects play: ball flies farther (thin air), body fatigues faster, greens firm up through the day. Strategy: take slightly less club in heat, stay hydrated (drink before you're thirsty), save energy where possible, expect firmer greens in afternoon. Physical management is part of course management on hot days.

title: Mental Reset After Bad Hole
body: Bad holes happen. Mental reset process: 1) Accept what happened—don't dwell. 2) Take deep breaths walking to next tee. 3) Positive self-talk: 'next shot is a new opportunity.' 4) Refocus on process, not outcome. 5) Start fresh with your routine. Carrying frustration forward compounds problems. Each hole is independent.

title: Playing to Your Strengths
body: Effective strategy leverages your strengths and protects weaknesses. Good driver? Use it on wide holes. Strong iron player? Lay up to your favorite distance. Great putter? Be aggressive getting on green even if farther from pin. Know what you do well and create opportunities for those shots. Minimize exposure to weaknesses.

title: Expected Score Thinking
body: Expected score is the average strokes to hole out from your position. Example: from fairway 150 yards out, your expected score might be 3.2. From rough, it might be 3.5. Decisions should minimize expected score, not maximize chance of best outcome. Think: what's my average result? Not: what's possible if I hit it perfect?

title: When to Regrip Clubs
body: Grips wear out, losing tackiness and affecting control. Signs to regrip: slick/hard feel, visible wear/shine, grip spinning in hand. Frequency: once per year for regular players (40+ rounds), more often in hot/humid climates or if you wear gloves out quickly. Fresh grips improve confidence and performance significantly for minimal cost.

title: Using Launch Monitors
body: Launch monitors measure: club speed, ball speed, launch angle, spin rate, carry distance, and more. Use for: club fitting (find optimal specifications), practice feedback (see effects of changes), course preparation (dial in distances). Don't obsess over numbers during practice—use them diagnostically. Technology helps but feel still matters.

title: Using Rangefinder Effectively
body: Rangefinders provide exact yardages. Best practices: get distance to front, middle, and back of green; get distance to hazards and layup targets; account for elevation (some models do this). Don't: take so long measuring that you slow play. Know your numbers and be ready to hit. Technology assists but doesn't replace decision making.

title: What to Expect in a Fitting
body: Club fitting process: 1) Interview about your game and goals. 2) Baseline shots with current clubs. 3) Test different heads, shafts, configurations. 4) Launch monitor comparison of options. 5) Final recommendation. Good fitters explain why options work for you. Budget: $50-150 for fitting, then club cost. Time: 1-2 hours for full bag.

title: Index vs Course Handicap
body: Handicap Index is your portable handicap number. Course Handicap is that index adjusted for specific course difficulty (slope rating). Course Handicap = Index × (Slope/113). Example: 15 Index on 130 slope course = 17.3 Course Handicap. Always use Course Handicap for competition at a specific course. Index stays the same; Course Handicap varies.

title: Net vs Gross Score
body: Gross score is your actual strokes taken. Net score is gross minus your Course Handicap. Net score is used for handicapped competitions to level the field. Example: you shoot 92 gross with 18 Course Handicap = 74 net. Net even par (72) is the target. Improvement is measured by lowering both gross average and handicap index.

title: Stableford Scoring
body: Stableford awards points based on score relative to par: double bogey or worse = 0, bogey = 1, par = 2, birdie = 3, eagle = 4. Higher points win. Advantage: blow-up holes don't destroy rounds—just pick up and take 0. Modified Stableford varies point values. Good format for casual play or when wanting to reduce frustration.

title: Score Differential Explained
body: Score Differential is your adjusted gross score compared to course/slope rating. Formula: (Score - Course Rating) × 113 / Slope Rating. Example: score 85 on course rated 72.0/130 = (85-72) × 113/130 = 11.3 differential. Your Index uses best 8 of last 20 differentials. Lower differential = better performance relative to course difficulty.

title: Net Double Bogey Maximum
body: When posting scores, you can't take more than Net Double Bogey on any hole. Net Double Bogey = par + 2 + any handicap strokes you receive on that hole. Example: on a par 4 where you get 1 stroke, max you can post is 7. This prevents blow-up holes from artificially inflating handicap. Apply hole-by-hole when posting.

title: Value of Playing Lessons
body: Playing lessons differ from range lessons. Instructor watches you on course, observing: course management decisions, routine consistency, mental responses, specialty shots. You learn to take your range game to course. Often more valuable than swing instruction for mid-handicappers. Consider: one playing lesson equals value of several range sessions.

title: Practicing with Others
body: Practicing with peers adds motivation and competition. Games: closest to pin contests, up-and-down challenges, putting for dollars. Benefits: simulates pressure, more fun, accountability. Caution: don't let social time replace focused practice. Balance: some sessions alone for concentrated work, some with others for competitive simulation.

title: Why Routines Matter
body: Pre-shot routines create consistency through repetition. Benefits: reduce variables, calm nerves, signal body to perform learned skill. Without routine: each shot becomes unique challenge, anxiety increases, performance varies. Build routine in practice; trust it on course. Same routine for pressure putts as practice putts. Routine is your anchor.

title: Full Commitment to Shots
body: Half-committed swings rarely succeed. Once you've decided club and target, commit 100%. Signs of non-commitment: tentative swing, last-second changes, steering the ball. Fix: trust your decision, make a confident swing, accept the result. If you can't commit, step back and reconsider. Better to change decision than swing with doubt.

title: Accepting Results
body: Golf requires accepting bad outcomes from good swings (and sometimes good outcomes from bad swings). You control process, not results. After each shot: brief evaluation, then move on. Dwelling on bad shots affects subsequent shots. Goal: process-focused mindset where you execute your best and accept whatever happens. This is the path to lower scores.

title: Patience on the Course
body: Golf rewards patience. Patience means: waiting for right shots rather than forcing, accepting that pars are good scores, not panicking after mistakes, trusting that consistent play produces results over 18 holes. Impatience leads to: hero shots from bad positions, compounding errors, frustration-induced poor swings. Play the long game within each round.

title: Using Statistics to Improve
body: Statistics reveal where you lose strokes. Process: 1) Track stats for 5-10 rounds. 2) Calculate: fairways %, GIR %, up-and-down %, putts/GIR, three-putt %. 3) Compare to benchmarks for your handicap. 4) Identify biggest gap. 5) Allocate practice time to that weakness. Data shows where improvement yields most strokes saved.

title: Planning for Your Worst Shot
body: Strategy should account for your worst shot, not your best. When choosing target: visualize your typical miss, then your occasional bad miss. Does the bad miss bring disaster? If yes, aim elsewhere. Example: if you occasionally block it 30 yards right, and water is 25 yards right of flag, aim left of center.

title: Iron Distance Gaps
body: Standard iron gaps are 10-15 yards between clubs. If your gaps are larger, consider: hybrid to replace long iron, checking lofts (may be stronger than expected), swing consistency issues. Smaller gaps can indicate: fitting opportunity, need to check lofts, or that your distances are already well-optimized. Know your gaps through range testing.

title: 5-Wood vs Hybrid: Which to Choose
body: 5-wood (18-19°): higher trajectory, more carry, better from tee. Hybrid (similar loft): lower trajectory, more versatile from rough, easier to hit from ground. Decision factors: do you need more fairway/rough versatility (hybrid) or tee/fairway distance (5-wood)? Many players carry both for different situations.

title: 7-Wood: The Overlooked Club
body: 7-wood (21-22°) is underrated for many players. Benefits: higher launch than hybrid for soft landings, easier to hit than long irons, versatile from fairway and light rough. Good replacement for: 3-4 hybrid or 3-4 iron for players who need higher flight. Consider if you struggle getting long clubs airborne.

title: Approach Wedge Role
body: Approach wedge (or gap wedge, 50-52°) fills the yardage gap between PW and SW. Essential for full shots in 95-115 yard range. Without it, you're either choking down on PW or full-swinging SW. Most modern sets need this wedge due to strong PW lofts. Treat it as a full-swing club, not just a specialty option.

title: 60-Degree Wedge Considerations
body: 60-degree lob wedge is specialty club with narrow margin for error. Best for: short-sided shots over bunkers, tight pins on firm greens. Risks: thin shots fly hole, fat shots go nowhere. Alternative: open 56° face for similar effect with more bounce protection. Don't carry 60° unless you practice with it regularly.

title: When to Club Down
body: Club down (use less club) situations: downwind, downhill, adrenaline pumping, firm greens with back pin, want to ensure ball doesn't go long. Also club down for control shots where accuracy matters more than distance. Mental note: amateurs more often need to club up, not down. Club down only with clear reason.

title: When to Club Up
body: Club up (use more club) situations: into wind, uphill, cold weather, wet conditions, front pin with room behind, tired late in round, you rarely go long. Most amateurs leave approaches short. When between clubs, default to more club and easier swing. Full distance with control beats maxed-out swing.

title: Long Approach Club Selection
body: Long approaches (180+ yards for most) require honest assessment. Can you reach green in regulation with acceptable risk? If forced long club hits water 30% of time, consider laying up to favorite wedge distance. Long clubs from rough are especially difficult. Sometimes strategic bogey beats disaster double or worse.

title: Short Iron Precision
body: Short irons (8, 9, PW) should be your most precise clubs. From 100-140 yards, you should be hitting greens at high percentage. If not, focus here first. Check: is ball position consistent? Is contact ball-first? Are distances known accurately? Short iron proficiency is the difference between birdie putts and scrambling.

title: Hybrid Setup Details
body: Hybrid setup: ball position like 5-iron (forward of center), hands slightly ahead, weight centered or slightly favoring lead side. Swing: more like iron than wood, descending blow with ball-first contact. Don't try to sweep it like a fairway wood. Trust the club's design to get ball airborne.

title: Club Selection Decision Tree
body: Club selection process: 1) Distance to target. 2) Wind adjustment (+/- clubs). 3) Lie adjustment (rough = less club, downhill = more club). 4) Green conditions (firm = land short, soft = attack). 5) Miss preferences (where can you miss?). 6) Confidence check (do you trust this club today?). Run through this for every approach.

title: Iron Forgiveness Features
body: Forgiving irons feature: larger clubhead, wider sole, more offset, perimeter weighting, lower CG, stronger lofts. Trade-offs: less workability, higher trajectory. Modern game-improvement irons rival mid-handicap player's irons of past. Don't let ego dictate—choose clubs that produce best results for your game. Forgiveness helps everyone.

title: Driver Face Materials
body: Driver faces are typically titanium alloy for optimal flex and durability. Variable thickness faces: thin center for max ball speed, thicker edges for structural integrity. Carbon fiber crowns save weight, allowing more placement in sole for forgiveness. Face cup construction extends flexibility to edge hits. Technology helps off-center hits perform better.

title: Getting Fit for Shafts
body: Shaft fitting matters more than head selection for many players. Fitting process: hit various flexes and weights while tracking launch monitor data. Look for: consistent ball speed, optimal launch/spin, tight dispersion. Key variables: flex, weight, torque, kick point. A fit shaft makes the head work better; a misfit shaft fights you.

title: Putter Fitting Elements
body: Putter fitting considers: length (eyes over ball), lie (sole flush at impact), head style (matches stroke), face insert (feel preference), grip size (hand size and feel), weight (green speed adjustment). Many golfers ignore putter fitting but it's your most-used club. A fit putter builds confidence and consistency.

title: Graphite vs Steel Iron Shafts
body: Steel shafts: heavier (90-130g), more consistent feel, less vibration dampening, preferred by better players for control. Graphite: lighter (50-80g), absorb more vibration, help slower swingers generate speed, increasingly popular at all skill levels. Modern graphite rivals steel consistency. Choice depends on your priorities: speed vs. control vs. comfort.

title: Hybrid vs Long Iron Comparison
body: For same loft, hybrids vs long irons differ: hybrids launch higher, are more forgiving, easier from rough. Long irons offer more workability, lower flight, preferred by fast swingers in wind. Most mid-high handicappers benefit from hybrids through 5-iron. Better players may prefer long irons for specific conditions. Test both and choose based on performance.

title: Ball Selection by Skill Level
body: Beginners/high handicaps: distance ball (two-piece), affordable, reduces slice/hook spin. Mid handicaps: balanced ball (three-piece), some spin control, decent feel. Low handicaps: tour ball (multi-layer), maximum spin control, workability. Match ball to your ability—tour balls won't help if you can't find fairways. Upgrade as skill improves.

title: Golf Glove Selection
body: Glove should fit snugly without bunching—like a second skin. Sizing: measure around knuckles, check length to fingertips. Cabretta leather: softest feel, less durable. Synthetic: more durable, often cooler. Rain gloves: tacky when wet. Replace gloves when hard or smooth—worn gloves affect grip security. Keep spare in bag.

title: Golf Shoe Features
body: Golf shoes provide stability and traction essential for consistent swings. Spiked vs spikeless: spikes give more traction, spikeless more versatile off course. Waterproofing matters in wet conditions. Fit: comfortable for 4+ hours of walking. Modern golf shoes combine performance with everyday style. Don't overlook footwear's impact on your game.

title: Alignment Aid Equipment
body: Alignment aids help with practice: alignment sticks (versatile), laser pointers, putting mirrors, alignment-marked balls. For putting: line on ball helps start line, mirror checks eye position. In bag: alignment stick is most versatile training aid. Use aids to build proper alignment habits that become automatic.

title: Spin Axis Tilt
body: Spin axis describes the tilt of the ball's rotation relative to horizontal. Perfectly horizontal = no curve. Tilted right = curves right (fade/slice). Tilted left = curves left (draw/hook). More tilt = more curve. Spin axis is determined by face-to-path angle at impact. Understanding this explains why club path and face angle create curve.

title: Peak Height and Ball Flight
body: Peak height (apex) affects how ball lands. Higher peak: steeper descent, more stopping power. Lower peak: shallower descent, more roll. Driver apex: 80-100 feet optimal for most. Iron apex varies by club. Control apex with: launch angle, spin rate, ball speed. Wind affects high-apex shots more. Adjust trajectory based on conditions.

title: Roll Out vs Carry
body: Roll out is ground distance after landing. Affected by: landing angle, spin, green firmness, slope. Driver roll: 20-40 yards typical. Wedge roll: minimal (few feet with spin). Knowing your roll helps with club selection: firm fairways mean more roll = less club needed. Course knowledge of typical roll conditions aids planning.

title: Lie Angle at Impact
body: Dynamic lie angle changes from address to impact due to shaft droop and swing mechanics. Too upright at impact: toe up, shots go left. Too flat: heel up, shots go right. Proper lie: sole flush, ball goes where aimed. Impact tape on sole shows your tendency. Dynamic fitting measures lie at impact, not just address.

title: Shaft Lean at Impact
body: Shaft lean describes the forward or backward angle of shaft at impact. Forward lean: hands ahead of clubhead, decreases effective loft, promotes ball-first contact. Backward lean: hands behind clubhead, increases loft, causes scoopy contact. Better players have forward lean with irons. Forward lean compresses ball for distance and control.

title: Ball Compression Explained
body: When club strikes ball, ball compresses against face then springs off. Higher compression balls require more speed to compress but maximize energy transfer at high speeds. Lower compression balls compress easier for slower swingers. Visible compression: ball flattens slightly at impact. The 'trampoline effect' of face flex adds to energy return.

title: Reading Your Divot
body: Divots reveal swing information. Direction: divot pointing left of target = out-to-in path; right = in-to-out. Depth: deep = steep angle, shallow = sweeping. Start point: should be after ball position. Toe marks indicate toe-first contact. No divot with irons usually indicates thin contact. Use divots to diagnose swing issues.

title: Offset Design Effects
body: Offset (clubface behind hosel) gives hands time to square face before impact. More offset = more help squaring face = fights slice. Progressive offset sets have more offset in long irons, less in short. Players clubs have minimal offset for workability. Match offset to your needs—don't fight your equipment.

title: Blade Length and Forgiveness
body: Blade length is the measurement across the clubface from heel to toe. Longer blade: larger hitting area, more forgiveness, more confidence at address. Shorter blade: more compact, preferred by better players for workability and appearance. Game improvement irons have longer blades; player's irons are more compact.

title: Top Line Thickness
body: Top line is the edge of clubface visible at address. Thin top line: cleaner look, less visual help, preferred by better players. Thick top line: more confidence-inspiring, frames the ball, common on game improvement irons. Top line is purely visual but affects confidence. Choose what looks good to your eye.

title: Optimal Trajectory Window
body: Each club has optimal launch and spin window for maximum distance. Driver example: 12-15° launch with 2000-2500rpm spin. Too high launch with too much spin = balloon. Too low with too little spin = nose dive. Finding your optimal window through fitting or launch monitor maximizes distance potential.

title: Iron Spin Rates
body: Iron spin rates create stopping power. Typical ranges: 7-iron 6500-7500rpm, 9-iron 8500-9500rpm, wedge 9000-11000rpm. Higher spin = more stop but more wind susceptibility. Lower spin = more roll. Control spin with: strike quality, shaft, ball choice, angle of attack. Track your spin to understand ball behavior on greens.

title: One-Length Iron Concept
body: One-length irons (like Cobra One Length) feature same shaft length throughout set (typically 7-iron length). Benefits: same setup, same swing feel, simpler. Trade-offs: long irons harder to hit (less length = less speed), short clubs may feel long. Works for some players, especially those who struggle with long iron setup differences.

title: Multiple Penalties on Same Act
body: When one action incurs multiple penalties, you typically only apply the highest penalty, not all of them. Example: accidentally moving ball while removing loose impediment might violate two rules, but you take one penalty, not two. Exception: some specific situations do add penalties. When in doubt, apply most applicable single penalty.

title: Serious Breach of Rules
body: Serious breach is playing from a significantly wrong place that gives major advantage. Example: dropping 50 yards closer to hole than allowed. Penalty: must correct error; if not corrected before starting next hole, disqualification in stroke play. Regular wrong place penalty is 2 strokes. Serious breach requires correction to avoid DQ.

title: Scorecard Responsibility
body: In stroke play, you're responsible for hole-by-hole scores on your card. Before signing: verify each hole score is correct. If you sign a score lower than actually taken: disqualification. Higher than taken: that higher score stands. Committee handles totaling. Mark card clearly, verify before signing. Your signature confirms accuracy.

title: Concession in Match Play
body: In match play, you may concede opponent's next stroke, hole, or match anytime before outcome is decided. Concession cannot be declined or withdrawn. Common: concede short putts to maintain pace. Strategy: don't concede anything you'd enjoy watching them miss. Gamesmanship: early concessions can make opponent uncomfortable when you stop conceding.

title: Play Ball as It Lies
body: Fundamental rule: play ball as it lies without improving conditions. Don't: press down ground, bend branches, move loose objects interfering with swing (except loose impediments). Do: take natural stance, make normal practice swing. If anything growing or fixed is disturbed during normal stroke, no penalty. Test of good sportsmanship is playing fair.

title: Preferred Lies (Winter Rules)
body: Preferred lies is a local rule allowing ball improvement in fairway (lift, clean, place within 6 inches or one club-length). Used in poor course conditions. Check scorecard or pro shop for local rules. When in effect, mark ball, lift, clean, place within prescribed distance, not nearer hole. Not always in effect—verify before using.

title: Playing Out of Turn
body: In stroke play, playing out of turn is not penalized—play continues. Ready golf is encouraged. In match play, opponent may recall your stroke played out of turn—you must replay without penalty. Use this strategically if opponent plays aggressive shot before you've even set up. Politely assert your right to proper order.

title: Damaged Clubs During Round
body: If club damaged during round by normal use, you may continue using it or have it repaired. If damaged by abuse (anger), you must continue using it damaged—cannot repair or replace. Lost club cannot be replaced. Damaged in normal course of play retains conforming status. Carry backup putter if yours is temperamental.

title: Interference with Swing or Stance
body: Interference exists when condition affects: ball position, intended stance, area of swing, intended line of play (putting green only). If any of these are affected, you may be entitled to relief. 'Might' affect is not enough—there must be actual interference with how you would reasonably play the shot.

title: Declaring Your Intentions
body: Some situations require declaring intentions: provisional ball ('I'm playing a provisional'), ball unplayable. Others require marking before lifting. State your intentions clearly so playing partners understand what you're doing. This prevents disputes. When using any relief procedure, verbalize your decision before acting.

title: Block vs Random Practice Deep Dive
body: Block practice: same shot repeatedly. Good for grooving new technique. Random practice: vary shots constantly. Better for skill transfer to course. Recommended: start session with block work on weak area, transition to random simulating course play. End with challenging random sequence. This combines technique work with game preparation.

title: Interleaved Practice Method
body: Interleaved practice alternates between different skills within a session instead of finishing one before starting another. Example: 5 drives, 5 chips, 5 putts, repeat. Feels harder but produces better retention and transfer. Your brain stays engaged by constantly switching tasks. Use for well-established skills needing sharpening.

title: Simulating Course Conditions
body: Practice that simulates course conditions transfers better. Methods: play imaginary holes (driver, approach, chip, putt in sequence), practice from different lies, create pressure (consequences for misses), vary targets constantly, include pre-shot routine every shot. Range practice should feel like course play, not robotic repetition.

title: Putting Games for Practice
body: Games make practice engaging and competitive. 'Around the world': make putts from 3 feet at 4 compass points, then 5 feet, etc. 'Safety drawback': if you miss, move ball back 1 putter length. 'Par 18': 9 holes, par 2 each, try to beat par. Games add pressure and purpose. Practice becomes play.

title: Chipping Games for Practice
body: Chipping games build competition and pressure. 'Up and down challenge': 10 random positions, count how many you get up and down. 'Closest to pin': compete with friend from same spots. 'Points game': inside 3 feet=2 points, 3-6 feet=1 point, play to 10. Make it fun, make it competitive, track progress.

title: Strategic Range Practice
body: Range strategy: arrive with specific goals, not 'hit balls.' Write 2-3 focus areas before starting. Example: 'Work on tempo, practice 150-yard shots, finish with confident driver.' Allocate time to each goal. Without plan, you'll revert to hitting favorite clubs. Treat range time as valuable training, not recreation.

title: Fixing a Fault in Practice
body: To fix a fault: 1) Identify specifically what's wrong (video helps). 2) Understand the cause (not just symptom). 3) Find one drill that addresses root cause. 4) Exaggerate the correction initially. 5) Gradually moderate to new normal. 6) Test under simulated pressure. Fixing takes focused repetition over days/weeks, not minutes.

title: Learning New Skills
body: Learning new techniques follows predictable path: 1) Understand concept intellectually. 2) Slow motion rehearsal. 3) Practice without ball. 4) Slow swings with ball. 5) Gradually increase speed. 6) Random practice. 7) Take to course. Don't skip steps—rushing creates poor habits. New skills take weeks to become automatic.

title: Maintaining Existing Skills
body: Maintenance practice keeps skills sharp without intensive work. For solid players: 30-minute sessions 2-3x per week covering all areas briefly. Focus shifts based on what felt off during last round. Goal: keep touch and timing, not rebuild technique. Separate maintenance practice from improvement practice.

title: Practice Mindset
body: Effective practice requires: intentionality (clear goals), focus (present attention), patience (skills take time), honesty (acknowledge weaknesses), discipline (do the work you need, not just want). Treat practice as work that pays dividends. Show up with purpose. Quality of attention matters more than quantity of time.

title: Afternoon Pin Positions
body: Course superintendent moves pins throughout week. Patterns: harder positions for tournaments, easier for casual play. Sunday afternoon pins are often in challenging spots from weekend play. Morning vs afternoon: foot traffic affects green smoothness near hole. Factor these elements into your approach strategy and expectations.

title: Reading Green Slopes for Approach
body: Before hitting approach, read green: where's the safe miss? Front-to-back slope means leave it below hole. Side slope: miss to uphill putt side. Identify collection areas to avoid. This reading influences target selection—sometimes center green isn't the smartest play. Think about the putt you want to leave.

title: Penalty Stroke Avoidance
body: One penalty stroke is recoverable; two or more devastates the hole. Strategy: avoid situations where penalty strokes compound. Example: OB requires stroke-and-distance (2 strokes lost essentially). Water allows better relief options. Aim away from OB with extra margin. Accept small miss penalties rather than risking catastrophic ones.

title: Uphill vs Downhill Approach
body: Uphill approaches: take more club (ball must climb), expect less roll, be aggressive to back of green okay. Downhill approaches: take less club, expect more roll, leave short is acceptable. Severe elevation changes can mean 2-3 clubs adjustment. Walk off courses are particularly affected. Factor elevation into every approach calculation.

title: Building Course Knowledge
body: Course knowledge accumulates over rounds. Track: distances that are dead zones, greens that don't hold, bunkers that are disaster, where wind usually comes from. Note which holes play harder/easier than expected. Over time, course knowledge provides huge advantage over visitors. Keep a course notebook for courses you play regularly.

title: Using Technology Strategically
body: GPS and rangefinders provide distance; you provide strategy. Beyond pin distance, gather: front/back of green, hazard carries, layup distances. Use this information strategically—knowing bunker is 230 means if you hit driver 240, choose different club. Technology removes guesswork but doesn't make decisions for you.

title: Building and Losing Momentum
body: Momentum is psychological but feels real. Build on good shots: maintain positive tempo, trust your swing. After bad shots: don't chase momentum with risky plays. Momentum shifts quickly—don't overreact to either direction. Best mindset: every shot is independent opportunity. Past shots don't determine future shots.

title: Distance vs Direction Priority
body: Most amateurs prioritize direction over distance—hitting it straight but short. Better strategy: prioritize distance with acceptable direction. A 150-yard slice is better than 120-yard straight ball. Work on fixing direction issues through practice, but don't sacrifice distance trying to steer on course. Let the club work.

title: Trusting Your Swing
body: Trust means committing to your swing without interference. Lack of trust causes: steering, decelerating, last-second changes, tension. Build trust through: quality practice, pre-shot routine, acceptance of outcomes. On course: trust what you brought that day. Save adjustments for practice. Trust is the foundation of good golf.
